LEXASSIST LEGAL QA — CONSTITUTIONAL LAW
============================================================

Q: What criteria did the Supreme Court highlight as necessary for the appointment of DGMS (Army)?
A: The Supreme Court highlighted that the criteria included inter se seniority and suitability, and that Maj. Gen. Manomoy Ganguly, being the senior most and suitable, should be promoted.
Case: Union of India vs. Maj. Gen. Manomoy Ganguly
Date: 1st August 2018

---

Q: What were the final instructions of the Supreme Court regarding the promotion of Maj. Gen. Manomoy Ganguly?
A: The Supreme Court instructed that Maj. Gen. Manomoy Ganguly should be appointed to the post of DGMS (Army) without further delay, in accordance with the AFT's decision.
Case: Union of India vs. Maj. Gen. Manomoy Ganguly
Date: 1st August 2018

---

Q: How did the High Court of Uttarakhand initially rule on the review application filed by the appellants in the case Davesh Nagalya (D) & Ors. vs. Pradeep Kumar (D) Thr. LRs. and Ors.?
A: The High Court of Uttarakhand dismissed the review application on 23rd April 2008, stating that the grounds urged were different from those in the writ petition, and did not consider the subsequent events such as the death of Pradeep Kumar.
Case: Davesh Nagalya (D) & Ors. vs. Pradeep Kumar (D) Thr. LRs. and Ors.
Date: 10th August 2021

---

Q: What was the final decision of the Supreme Court in the case Davesh Nagalya (D) & Ors. vs. Pradeep Kumar (D) Thr. LRs. and Ors.?
A: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order, deemed the tenancy to have ended with the death of the partners, and ruled that the non-residential tenanted premises is deemed to be vacant. The appellants were allowed to proceed with remedies available under the law.
Case: Davesh Nagalya (D) & Ors. vs. Pradeep Kumar (D) Thr. LRs. and Ors.
Date: 10th August 2021

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court decide regarding the dispute over Survey No.988 in the case Selvi vs. Gopalakrishnan Nair (D) Thr. LRs. and Ors.?
A: The Supreme Court set aside the judgments of the High Court and lower courts, and remitted the matter back to the trial court to decide afresh, allowing the parties to adduce evidence regarding the correct description of the suit property and the rights claimed by the second defendant in Survey No.988.
Case: Selvi vs. Gopalakrishnan Nair (D) Thr. LRs. and Ors.
Date: 15th May 2018

---

Q: What directions did the Supreme Court give to the trial court for further proceedings in the case Selvi vs. Gopalakrishnan Nair (D) Thr. LRs. and Ors.?
A: The Supreme Court directed the trial court to allow the parties to adduce evidence, ascertain the correct survey numbers falling within the description of the suit properties, and determine the entitlement of the second defendant to Survey No.988.
Case: Selvi vs. Gopalakrishnan Nair (D) Thr. LRs. and Ors.
Date: 15th May 2018

---

Q: Why did the Supreme Court dismiss the objections raised by the second plaintiff, Vasudevan Pillai, regarding the final decree application in the case Selvi vs. Gopalakrishnan Nair (D) Thr. LRs. and Ors.?
A: The Supreme Court dismissed Vasudevan Pillai's objections as an afterthought and upheld that third plaintiff Selvi had the right to pursue the final decree application, stating that Vasudevan Pillai's claims of forgery were not credible.
Case: Selvi vs. Gopalakrishnan Nair (D) Thr. LRs. and Ors.
Date: 15th May 2018

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court of India rule on the appeal in the case Shakti Bhog Food Industries Ltd. vs. The Central Bank of India & Anr.?
A: The Supreme Court of India set aside the judgments of the lower courts and the High Court, holding that the suit was within the limitation period based on the facts and circumstances of the case, and remitted the matter back for further proceedings.
Case: Shakti Bhog Food Industries Ltd. vs. The Central Bank of India & Anr.
Date: 5th June 2020

---

Q: What legal principle did the Supreme Court highlight regarding the interpretation of the limitation period in the case Shakti Bhog Food Industries Ltd. vs. The Central Bank of India & Anr.?
A: The Supreme Court highlighted that the expression 'when the right to sue accrues' under Article 113 of the Limitation Act, 1963, must be understood in the context of the specific facts and circumstances, indicating that the right to sue may accrue at different points of time based on the nature of the dispute and communications between the parties.
Case: Shakti Bhog Food Industries Ltd. vs. The Central Bank of India & Anr.
Date: 5th June 2020

---

Q: What did the High Court of Delhi rule regarding the sharing of live broadcasting signals in the case Union of India vs. Board of Control for Cricket in India & Ors.?
A: The High Court of Delhi ruled that the signals received by Prasar Bharati from BCCI should not be retransmitted by cable operators and that this retransmission was not covered under Section 8 of the Cable Act, 1995.
Case: Union of India vs. Board of Control for Cricket in India & Ors.
Date: 22nd August 2017

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court of India decide regarding the live broadcast signals shared by BCCI with Prasar Bharati in the case Union of India vs. Board of Control for Cricket in India & Ors.?
A: The Supreme Court of India upheld the High Court's decision and ruled that the live broadcast signals shared by BCCI with Prasar Bharati should not be retransmitted by cable operators. The court emphasized that the signals were meant for Prasar Bharati's terrestrial and DTH networks only.
Case: Union of India vs. Board of Control for Cricket in India & Ors.
Date: 22nd August 2017

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court interpret Section 3 of the Sports Broadcasting Signals (Mandatory Sharing with Prasar Bharati) Act, 2007 in the case Union of India vs. Board of Control for Cricket in India & Ors.?
A: The Supreme Court interpreted Section 3 of the Sports Act, 2007 as mandating that the live broadcast signals shared with Prasar Bharati should be retransmitted only on Prasar Bharati's terrestrial and DTH networks, and not through cable operators.
Case: Union of India vs. Board of Control for Cricket in India & Ors.
Date: 22nd August 2017

---

Q: What was the stance of the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) regarding the retransmission of live signals by cable operators in the case Union of India vs. Board of Control for Cricket in India & Ors.?
A: BCCI argued that retransmitting the live signals through cable operators without proper authorization infringed on their broadcasting rights and revenue, as these signals were exclusively licensed to specific broadcasters under the Media Rights Agreement.
Case: Union of India vs. Board of Control for Cricket in India & Ors.
Date: 22nd August 2017

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court say about the balance between public access to sports and the rights of content owners in the case Union of India vs. Board of Control for Cricket in India & Ors.?
A: The Supreme Court acknowledged the need to balance public access to sports events with the rights of content owners, but ultimately ruled that the statutory mandate under the Sports Act, 2007 should be strictly interpreted to limit retransmission to Prasar Bharati's networks.
Case: Union of India vs. Board of Control for Cricket in India & Ors.
Date: 22nd August 2017

---

Q: Who facilitated the mediation efforts in the case Anu Bhandari vs. Pradip Bhandari?
A: The mediation efforts were facilitated by Hon'ble Mrs. Justice Lisa Gill, Judge of the High Court of Punjab and Haryana, and Ms. Meenakshi Arora, learned Senior Counsel, appointed by the Supreme Court as a Mediator.
Case: Anu Bhandari vs. Pradip Bhandari
Date: 5th March 2018

---

Q: What was the outcome of the mediation efforts in the case Anu Bhandari vs. Pradip Bhandari?
A: The mediation efforts led to an amicable settlement between the parties, resulting in the resolution of all their disputes and the filing of a mutual consent divorce petition.
Case: Anu Bhandari vs. Pradip Bhandari
Date: 5th March 2018

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court address the future litigation between Anu Bhandari and Pradip Bhandari?
A: The Supreme Court restrained both parties from instituting any fresh litigation in respect of the subject matter without the Court's leave.
Case: Anu Bhandari vs. Pradip Bhandari
Date: 5th March 2018

---

Q: What role did the Supreme Court play in facilitating the settlement in the case Anu Bhandari vs. Pradip Bhandari?
A: The Supreme Court actively facilitated the settlement through mediation and directed the parties to appear before it, leading to the resolution of disputes and the grant of mutual consent divorce.
Case: Anu Bhandari vs. Pradip Bhandari
Date: 5th March 2018

---

Q: Why did the High Court set aside the trial court's judgment in the case Akhilesh Singh @ Akhileshwar Singh vs. Lal Babu Singh & Ors.?
A: The High Court set aside the trial court's judgment after accepting additional evidence, which included sale deeds indicating that a partition had already occurred in the family. The High Court ruled that there was no unity of title and possession between the parties based on this evidence.
Case: Akhilesh Singh @ Akhileshwar Singh vs. Lal Babu Singh & Ors.
Date: 21st February 2018

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's ruling regarding the High Court's acceptance of additional evidence in the case Akhilesh Singh @ Akhileshwar Singh vs. Lal Babu Singh & Ors.?
A: The Supreme Court ruled that the High Court should have given the appellant an opportunity to rebut the additional evidence or explain the alleged admissions in the sale deeds. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment and remanded the case for fresh consideration.
Case: Akhilesh Singh @ Akhileshwar Singh vs. Lal Babu Singh & Ors.
Date: 21st February 2018

---

Q: What procedural error did the High Court commit according to the Supreme Court in the case Akhilesh Singh @ Akhileshwar Singh vs. Lal Babu Singh & Ors.?
A: The procedural error committed by the High Court was that it admitted additional evidence and proceeded to decide the appeal without giving the appellant an opportunity to rebut the additional evidence or explain the alleged admissions, thereby violating the principles of natural justice.
Case: Akhilesh Singh @ Akhileshwar Singh vs. Lal Babu Singh & Ors.
Date: 21st February 2018

---

Q: How did the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) respond to Vikash Kumar's request for a scribe?
A: The UPSC rejected Vikash Kumar's request for a scribe on the grounds that he did not meet the criteria of having a benchmark disability as defined under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016.
Case: Vikash Kumar vs. Union Public Service Commission & Ors.
Date: 11th February 2021

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's view on the interpretation of 'benchmark disability' in the context of providing a scribe?
A: The Supreme Court held that the provision of a scribe should not be limited to candidates with benchmark disabilities and emphasized that reasonable accommodation must be made for all persons with disabilities, including those with specific disabilities like Writer's Cramp.
Case: Vikash Kumar vs. Union Public Service Commission & Ors.
Date: 11th February 2021

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court say about the obligation of examining bodies under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016?
A: The Supreme Court stated that examining bodies have an obligation to provide reasonable accommodations, such as the assistance of a scribe, to candidates with disabilities to ensure their full and effective participation in examinations.
Case: Vikash Kumar vs. Union Public Service Commission & Ors.
Date: 11th February 2021

---

Q: What directive did the Supreme Court give to the UPSC regarding Vikash Kumar's case?
A: The Supreme Court directed the UPSC to reconsider Vikash Kumar's request for a scribe in light of the broader interpretation of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, and to make necessary accommodations for his disability.
Case: Vikash Kumar vs. Union Public Service Commission & Ors.
Date: 11th February 2021

---

Q: What was the primary legal issue in the case Apollo Institute of Medical Sciences & Research vs. Union of India & Anr.?
A: The primary legal issue was whether the Central Government's decision to debar the petitioner's medical college from admitting students for two years and to encash the bank guarantee was justified.
Case: Apollo Institute of Medical Sciences & Research vs. Union of India & Anr.
Date: 31st August 2017

---

Q: What role did the Oversight Committee (OC) play in the case Apollo Institute of Medical Sciences & Research vs. Union of India & Anr.?
A: The OC, constituted under the Supreme Court's directions, reviewed the compliance submitted by the college and initially approved the scheme for the academic session 2016-17, but later noted deficiencies in subsequent inspections.
Case: Apollo Institute of Medical Sciences & Research vs. Union of India & Anr.
Date: 31st August 2017

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's view on the deficiencies noted by the Medical Council of India in the case Apollo Institute of Medical Sciences & Research vs. Union of India & Anr.?
A: The Supreme Court observed that the deficiencies noted by MCI were marginal and that the Central Government's decision to debar the college for two years was excessive. The court emphasized the need for proportionality in administrative decisions.
Case: Apollo Institute of Medical Sciences & Research vs. Union of India & Anr.
Date: 31st August 2017

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court rule on the issue of admitting students for the academic session 2017-18 in the case Apollo Institute of Medical Sciences & Research vs. Union of India & Anr.?
A: The Supreme Court set aside the Central Government's decision to debar the college from admitting students for two years and allowed the college to admit students for the academic session 2017-18, subject to fulfilling conditions imposed by the Oversight Committee.
Case: Apollo Institute of Medical Sciences & Research vs. Union of India & Anr.
Date: 31st August 2017

---

Q: What directive did the Supreme Court give regarding future inspections of Apollo Institute of Medical Sciences & Research?
A: The Supreme Court allowed the Medical Council of India or the Competent Authority of the Central Government to inspect the college as deemed fit and to take appropriate action if any deficiencies were found in the future, after giving the college an opportunity to address them.
Case: Apollo Institute of Medical Sciences & Research vs. Union of India & Anr.
Date: 31st August 2017

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's final decision in the case Apollo Institute of Medical Sciences & Research vs. Union of India & Anr.?
A: The Supreme Court quashed the decision to debar the college from admitting students and extended the cut-off date for admissions to 5th September 2017, allowing the college to participate in the ongoing counselling process for the academic session 2017-18.
Case: Apollo Institute of Medical Sciences & Research vs. Union of India & Anr.
Date: 31st August 2017

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's response to Ms. Indira Jaising's request to expunge the remarks made against her?
A: The Supreme Court observed that the remarks were made in the context of the conduct of the petitioners and intervenors collectively and were based on the arguments presented during the hearing. The court did not find a basis to expunge the remarks specifically against Ms. Jaising.
Case: Tehseen Poonawalla vs. Union of India & Anr.
Date: 26th September 2018

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court say about the inclusion of prayer clause (c) in Ms. Indira Jaising's Miscellaneous Application?
A: The Supreme Court noted that prayer clause (c), which sought records from the High Court of Bombay regarding the transfer of Judge Utpat, was indicative of an attempt to revive the controversy settled by the earlier judgment. Dr. Singhvi later submitted that this prayer was being given up.
Case: Tehseen Poonawalla vs. Union of India & Anr.
Date: 26th September 2018

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's final decision regarding the Miscellaneous Application filed by Ms. Indira Jaising?
A: The Supreme Court disposed of the Miscellaneous Application, maintaining the remarks made in the judgment and stating that they pertained to the collective conduct of the petitioners and intervenors, including Ms. Jaising.
Case: Tehseen Poonawalla vs. Union of India & Anr.
Date: 26th September 2018

---

Q: What was the High Court's decision regarding the deductions claimed by M/s. Saraf Exports under Section 80-IB?
A: The High Court held that M/s. Saraf Exports was not entitled to the deductions under Section 80-IB for the profits from Duty Drawback and DEPB schemes, based on the judgments of the Supreme Court in Liberty India and Sterling Foods.
Case: M/s. Saraf Exports vs. Commissioner of Income Tax, Jaipur-III
Date: 10th April 2023

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's decision on the appeal filed by M/s. Saraf Exports?
A: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's decision that the profits from Duty Drawback and DEPB schemes are not eligible for deductions under Section 80-IB as they do not constitute profits derived from the industrial undertaking.
Case: M/s. Saraf Exports vs. Commissioner of Income Tax, Jaipur-III
Date: 10th April 2023

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court differentiate between the cases of Liberty India and Meghalaya Steels?
A: The Supreme Court distinguished that while Liberty India dealt with export incentives like DEPB and Duty Drawback, which have an indirect nexus with the industrial undertaking, Meghalaya Steels involved subsidies directly reducing the cost of manufacturing, thus having a direct nexus.
Case: M/s. Saraf Exports vs. Commissioner of Income Tax, Jaipur-III
Date: 10th April 2023

---

Q: What was the final outcome for M/s. Saraf Exports regarding the deductions under Section 80-IB?
A: The final outcome was that M/s. Saraf Exports was not entitled to claim deductions under Section 80-IB for the profits earned from the Duty Drawback and DEPB schemes, as per the Supreme Court's ruling.
Case: M/s. Saraf Exports vs. Commissioner of Income Tax, Jaipur-III
Date: 10th April 2023

---

Q: How did the High Court of Delhi rule on the Section 34 petition filed by Ssangyong Engineering & Construction Co. Ltd.?
A: The High Court of Delhi dismissed the Section 34 petition, holding that the majority arbitral award was a possible view and that there was no ground for interference under the parameters of challenge to arbitral awards.
Case: Ssangyong Engineering & Construction Co. Ltd. vs. National Highways Authority of India (NHAI)
Date: 8th May 2019

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court address the issue of natural justice in the arbitration proceedings?
A: The Supreme Court noted that the arbitral tribunal's reliance on government guidelines, which were not presented to the parties, violated the principles of natural justice, as Ssangyong Engineering was not given an opportunity to address these guidelines.
Case: Ssangyong Engineering & Construction Co. Ltd. vs. National Highways Authority of India (NHAI)
Date: 8th May 2019

---

Q: What was the primary issue in the case World College of Medical Sciences & Research and Hospital vs. Union of India & Anr.?
A: The primary issue was whether the order passed by the Union of India, debarring the petitioner medical college from admitting students for two academic sessions (2017-18 and 2018-19) and authorizing the Medical Council of India (MCI) to encash the bank guarantee of Rs. 2 crore, was justified.
Case: World College of Medical Sciences & Research and Hospital vs. Union of India & Anr.
Date: 5th September 2017

---

Q: Why did the Union of India debar the petitioner medical college from admitting students?
A: The Union of India debarred the petitioner medical college based on the recommendation from the MCI, which noted several deficiencies in the college during an assessment conducted on 26th-27th October 2016.
Case: World College of Medical Sciences & Research and Hospital vs. Union of India & Anr.
Date: 5th September 2017

---

Q: What were the specific deficiencies noted by the MCI in the petitioner medical college?
A: The MCI noted deficiencies such as a 29.23% shortage of faculty, a 28.26% shortage of residents, 34% bed occupancy on the day of assessment, and other issues such as a lack of patients in ICUs and inadequate library facilities.
Case: World College of Medical Sciences & Research and Hospital vs. Union of India & Anr.
Date: 5th September 2017

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court address the argument about the timing of the inspection close to the Diwali festival?
A: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, noting that the inspection on 26th October 2016, which was three days before Diwali, did not violate the regulations prohibiting inspections two days before or after major festivals.
Case: World College of Medical Sciences & Research and Hospital vs. Union of India & Anr.
Date: 5th September 2017

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court decide regarding the future of the students already admitted to the petitioner medical college?
A: The Supreme Court allowed the students already admitted for the academic session 2016-17 to continue their studies but declined to issue directions for renewal of LOP for the academic session 2017-18. The Court directed the MCI to inspect the college for the academic session 2018-19 and submit a report.
Case: World College of Medical Sciences & Research and Hospital vs. Union of India & Anr.
Date: 5th September 2017

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's final directive to the MCI and the petitioner college?
A: The Supreme Court directed the MCI to conduct a fresh inspection within two months, inform the college of any deficiencies, and allow the college time to rectify them. The renewal application for 2017-18 was to be treated as an application for 2018-19, and the bank guarantee was not to be encashed until further orders.
Case: World College of Medical Sciences & Research and Hospital vs. Union of India & Anr.
Date: 5th September 2017

---

Q: What is meant by a 'speaking order' as directed by the Supreme Court in Avtar Singh's case?
A: A 'speaking order' is a detailed order in which the Appointing Authority must provide reasons for their decision after considering all relevant factors and giving Avtar Singh an opportunity to be heard.
Case: Avtar Singh vs. Union of India and Ors.
Date: 15th November 2017

---

Q: Why did the High Court reverse the decision of the Central Administrative Tribunal in Shri Ram Shridhar Chimurkar's case?
A: The High Court reversed the CAT's decision, stating that Rule 54(14)(b) of the CCS (Pension) Rules did not cover adoption by a widow after the death of a government servant and that the appellant could not be included in the definition of 'family' for receiving family pension.
Case: Shri Ram Shridhar Chimurkar vs. Union of India & Anr.
Date: 17th January 2023

---

Q: What is the significance of Section 8 and Section 12 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, in this case?
A: Section 8 of the HAMA Act allows a Hindu widow to adopt a child, and Section 12 states that an adopted child is deemed to be the child of the adoptive parents for all purposes. However, the Supreme Court found that these provisions did not apply to the entitlement of family pension under the CCS (Pension) Rules.
Case: Shri Ram Shridhar Chimurkar vs. Union of India & Anr.
Date: 17th January 2023

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court interpret the phrase 'in relation to a government servant' in Rule 54(14)(b) of the CCS (Pension) Rules?
A: The Supreme Court interpreted the phrase 'in relation to a government servant' to mean that the family member must have had a close and direct nexus with the deceased government servant during his lifetime. Therefore, a child adopted by the widow after the government servant's death could not be included.
Case: Shri Ram Shridhar Chimurkar vs. Union of India & Anr.
Date: 17th January 2023

---

Q: What was the primary issue in the case Dinganglung Gangmei vs. Mutum Churamani Meetei & Ors.?
A: The primary issue was whether the Acting Chief Justice of the High Court of Manipur had jurisdiction to issue directions to the Government of Manipur to respond to a communication regarding the inclusion of the Meitei community in the Presidential List of Scheduled Tribes.
Case: Dinganglung Gangmei vs. Mutum Churamani Meetei & Ors.
Date: 7th August 2023

---

Q: What action by the High Court of Manipur led to the filing of the Special Leave Petition in the Supreme Court?
A: The High Court of Manipur, on 27th March 2023, directed the Government of Manipur to recommend the inclusion of the Meitei community in the Presidential List of Scheduled Tribes within a stipulated time frame.
Case: Dinganglung Gangmei vs. Mutum Churamani Meetei & Ors.
Date: 7th August 2023

---

Q: What was the Union Government's position on the High Court's order regarding the Meitei community?
A: The Union Government stated that the State of Manipur was taking appropriate steps to recall the order of the Single Judge of the High Court dated 27th March 2023 by moving the competent forum.
Case: Dinganglung Gangmei vs. Mutum Churamani Meetei & Ors.
Date: 7th August 2023

---

Q: What measures did the Union Government report to the Supreme Court to address the situation in Manipur?
A: The Union Government reported deploying 52 companies of Central Armed Police Forces, 105 columns of the Army/Assam Rifles, conducting flag marches, appointing a Security Adviser, and setting up relief camps among other measures to ensure normalcy and provide relief in Manipur.
Case: Dinganglung Gangmei vs. Mutum Churamani Meetei & Ors.
Date: 7th August 2023

---

Q: What concerns did the petitioners express regarding the situation in Manipur?
A: The petitioners expressed concerns about threats to safety, the need for enhanced security in sensitive areas, and the overall law and order situation, seeking directions for relief and rehabilitation measures.
Case: Dinganglung Gangmei vs. Mutum Churamani Meetei & Ors.
Date: 7th August 2023

---

Q: What directions did the Supreme Court give to the authorities regarding the relief camps in Manipur?
A: The Supreme Court directed the authorities to ensure that relief camps provide all basic amenities, including food and medical care, and to take necessary precautions for the rehabilitation of displaced persons.
Case: Dinganglung Gangmei vs. Mutum Churamani Meetei & Ors.
Date: 7th August 2023

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's stance on the investigation and accountability of the violence in Manipur?
A: The Supreme Court emphasized the need for a thorough and impartial investigation into the violence, including sexual violence against women, and directed the appointment of a Special Investigation Team (SIT) to ensure proper investigation and accountability.
Case: Dinganglung Gangmei vs. Mutum Churamani Meetei & Ors.
Date: 7th August 2023

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court conclude regarding the classification of MVAC as a heat pump?
A: The Supreme Court concluded that MVAC did not satisfy the definition of a heat pump under the HSN, as its primary purpose was to produce chilled water, and the production of hot water was incidental. Thus, MVAC was not classified as a heat pump but as a refrigerating equipment under Sub-heading 8418.10 of the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985.
Case: M/s Thermax Ltd. vs. Commissioner of Central Excise, Pune-1
Date: 13th October 2022

---

Q: What was the significance of the market parlance test in this case?
A: The market parlance test indicated that the product was recognized and purchased as a vapour absorption chiller used for air conditioning and refrigeration, not as a heat pump. The Supreme Court noted that the appellant's website separately identified vapour absorption chillers and heat pumps, reinforcing this distinction.
Case: M/s Thermax Ltd. vs. Commissioner of Central Excise, Pune-1
Date: 13th October 2022

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court address the argument related to similar products by Blue Star Ltd. and Voltas Ltd.?
A: The Supreme Court found that the previous decisions regarding Blue Star Ltd. and Voltas Ltd. were not directly applicable, as they dealt with different issues and classifications. The classification dispute in this case was resolved based on the specific facts and definitions applicable to MVAC.
Case: M/s Thermax Ltd. vs. Commissioner of Central Excise, Pune-1
Date: 13th October 2022

---

Q: What did the High Court decide on the appeal by Siddamsetty Infra Projects Pvt. Ltd.?
A: The High Court partly allowed the appeal, holding that the purchaser was entitled to specific performance of the sale agreements and directed the appellants to execute the sale deed for the suit property to the extent of 90% of the total sale consideration already paid by the purchaser.
Case: Smt. Katta Sujatha Reddy & Anr. vs. Siddamsetty Infra Projects Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
Date: 25th August 2022

---

Q: How did the High Court of Uttarakhand at Nainital rule on the writ petition filed by Mohd. Inam?
A: The High Court of Uttarakhand allowed the writ petition filed by the landlords, upholding the declaration of vacancy and the order of possession in favor of the landlords.
Case: Mohd. Inam vs. Sanjay Kumar Singhal & Ors.
Date: 26th June 2020

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's view on the maintainability of the revision petition under Section 18 of the U.P. Act, 1972?
A: The Supreme Court held that the revision petition was maintainable and that the revisional authority had the jurisdiction to entertain the petition against the order declaring the premises as vacant.
Case: Mohd. Inam vs. Sanjay Kumar Singhal & Ors.
Date: 26th June 2020

---

Q: What was the final decision of the Supreme Court in this case?
A: The Supreme Court set aside the judgment of the High Court, restoring the order of the District Judge which had set aside the vacancy order and the final order of release. The Court held that the premises were not sub-let and that Mohd. Inam and his family were lawful tenants.
Case: Mohd. Inam vs. Sanjay Kumar Singhal & Ors.
Date: 26th June 2020

---

Q: What principle did the Supreme Court rely on in deciding whether the High Court should have entertained the application for revocation of leave?
A: The Supreme Court relied on the principle that questions of territorial jurisdiction should typically be raised in the written statement as part of the defense and not through an application for revocation of leave, as established in the cases of Secretary of State vs. Golabrai Paliram and Indian Mineral & Chemicals Co. vs. Deutsche Bank.
Case: Isha Distribution House Pvt. Ltd. vs. Aditya Birla Nuvo Ltd. & Anr.
Date: 7th March 2019

---

Q: What were the arguments made by the petitioners against the NLAT?
A: The petitioners argued that the admission notification for NLAT was in breach of statutory provisions, as it was issued without the recommendation of the Academic Council of NLSIU. They also contended that NLSIU, being a member of the Consortium of National Law Universities, was obligated to admit students through CLAT.
Case: Rakesh Kumar Agarwalla & Anr. vs. National Law School of India University, Bengaluru & Ors.
Date: 21st September 2020

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's view on the maintainability of the writ petition filed by Rakesh Kumar Agarwalla & Anr.?
A: The Supreme Court held that the writ petition was maintainable, considering the credentials of petitioner No.2, a former Vice-Chancellor of NLSIU, who was competent to espouse the cause of legal education.
Case: Rakesh Kumar Agarwalla & Anr. vs. National Law School of India University, Bengaluru & Ors.
Date: 21st September 2020

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's decision regarding the statutory requirements for issuing the NLAT notification?
A: The Supreme Court held that the NLAT notification was issued without the recommendation of the Academic Council, which is the statutory authority under the Act, 1986, for admission of students. Hence, the notification was not in accordance with statutory provisions.
Case: Rakesh Kumar Agarwalla & Anr. vs. National Law School of India University, Bengaluru & Ors.
Date: 21st September 2020

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's final ruling in this case?
A: The Supreme Court set aside the NLAT notification and directed NLSIU to admit students through the CLAT examination scheduled for 28th September 2020, ensuring adherence to the statutory provisions of the Act, 1986.
Case: Rakesh Kumar Agarwalla & Anr. vs. National Law School of India University, Bengaluru & Ors.
Date: 21st September 2020

---

Q: What relief did Adani Ports seek from the Supreme Court regarding their disqualification?

Q: What was the main legal issue in the case Abid-Ul-Islam vs. Inder Sain Dua?

Case: Abid-Ul-Islam vs. Inder Sain Dua
Date: 7th April 2022

---

Q: What was the High Court's reasoning for allowing the revision and granting leave to defend?

Case: Abid-Ul-Islam vs. Inder Sain Dua
Date: 7th April 2022

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court say about the High Court's exercise of revisional jurisdiction in this case?
A: The Supreme Court stated that the High Court had overstepped its revisional jurisdiction, which is limited to ensuring that the Rent Controller's order is according to law, without substituting its own findings for those of the Rent Controller.
Case: Abid-Ul-Islam vs. Inder Sain Dua
Date: 7th April 2022

Q: What was the Supreme Court's final decision regarding the order of the High Court?

Q: How did the Uttarakhand High Court rule on the appellants' writ petitions?
A: The Uttarakhand High Court rejected the appellants' writ petitions, holding that Statute No. 16.24 applied to the teachers of the university, but it did not entitle them to continue in service beyond the end of the month in which they attained the age of superannuation.
Case: Navin Chandra Dhoundiyal vs. State of Uttarakhand & Ors.
Date: 16th October 2020

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's view on the interpretation of Statute No. 16.24?
A: The Supreme Court held that the proviso to Statute No. 16.24 allowed teachers whose date of superannuation did not fall on 30th June to continue in service till the end of the academic session, i.e., 30th June following, treating them as re-employed from the date immediately following their superannuation till 30th June.
Case: Navin Chandra Dhoundiyal vs. State of Uttarakhand & Ors.
Date: 16th October 2020

---

Q: What reasoning did the Supreme Court provide for its interpretation of Statute No. 16.24?
A: The Supreme Court reasoned that the intent of the proviso was to avoid disruption in teaching caused by the discontinuity of service of a teaching staff member mid-session, and to ensure the academic needs of students were not adversely affected.
Case: Navin Chandra Dhoundiyal vs. State of Uttarakhand & Ors.
Date: 16th October 2020

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's final decision regarding the appellants' service continuation?
A: The Supreme Court set aside the impugned judgment and orders of the High Court, allowing the appellants to continue in service till the end of June following their superannuation on a re-employment basis. It also directed that any superannuated appellants should be reinstated with full salary for the period they were out of employment.
Case: Navin Chandra Dhoundiyal vs. State of Uttarakhand & Ors.
Date: 16th October 2020

---

Q: What were the grounds of appeal raised by the appellant before the Supreme Court?
A: The appellant argued that the fees and expenses were in accordance with the technical and financial bid approved by the CoC, and that the NCLT and NCLAT failed to apply their minds to the basis of the claim and the agreed figures.

---

Case: Devarajan Raman vs. Bank of India Limited
Date: 5th January 2022

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's final decision in this case?
A: The Supreme Court set aside the orders of the NCLT and NCLAT, and remanded the case back to the NCLT for a fresh decision on the appellant's claim for fees and costs, directing the NCLT to expedite the disposal of the matter within one month.

Q: What reasoning did the Supreme Court provide for rejecting the High Court's attribution of constructive notice to Mrs. Umadevi Nambiar?
A: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's attribution of constructive notice to Mrs. Umadevi Nambiar, stating that the possession of the agent under the Power of Attorney is also the possession of the principal, and any unauthorized sale by the agent does not amount to the principal parting with possession.

Date: 1st April 2022

Date: 1st April 2022

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's observation regarding the legislative intent behind section 153A?
A: The Supreme Court observed that the legislative intent behind section 153A was to bring to tax the total income, including any undisclosed income found during a search, but it did not intend to permit roving inquiries into completed assessments in the absence of any incriminating material found during the search.
Case: Principal Commissioner of Income Tax, Central-3 vs. Abhisar Buildwell P. Ltd.
Date: 24th April 2023

---

Q: What was the final decision of the Supreme Court in this case?
A: The Supreme Court held that in respect of completed/unabated assessments, no addition can be made if no incriminating material is found during the search, thereby dismissing the appeals filed by the Revenue.
Case: Principal Commissioner of Income Tax, Central-3 vs. Abhisar Buildwell P. Ltd.
Date: 24th April 2023

---

Q: What precedent did the Supreme Court rely on for its decision?
A: The Supreme Court relied on precedents set by various High Courts, including the Delhi High Court in the case of Kabul Chawla and the Gujarat High Court in the case of Saumya Construction, which held that no addition can be made in respect of completed/unabated assessments without incriminating material found during the search.
Case: Principal Commissioner of Income Tax, Central-3 vs. Abhisar Buildwell P. Ltd.
Date: 24th April 2023

---

Q: What is the significance of the Supreme Court's decision in this case?
A: The significance of the Supreme Court's decision is that it clarifies the interpretation of section 153A, limiting the scope of assessments to incriminating material found during searches, thus providing protection to taxpayers against unnecessary reopening of completed assessments.
Case: Principal Commissioner of Income Tax, Central-3 vs. Abhisar Buildwell P. Ltd.
Date: 24th April 2023

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's observation regarding the relationship between the nature of the duty and the measure of the levy?
A: The Supreme Court observed that excise is a levy on manufacture and the measure of the levy (i.e., the value) must have a nexus with the essential character of the levy. The measure can include value additions and other charges that enhance the product's value until its clearance.
Case: Commissioner of Central Excise, Indore vs. M/S Grasim Industries Ltd.
Date: 11th May 2018

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's decision regarding the inclusion of charges in the transaction value?
A: The Supreme Court held that charges such as packing, wear and tear, facility, service, delivery and collection, rental, repair, and testing charges can be included in the transaction value for the purpose of excise duty as they enhance the value of the product until its clearance.
Case: Commissioner of Central Excise, Indore vs. M/S Grasim Industries Ltd.
Date: 11th May 2018

---

Q: What was the outcome of the appeal filed by the DDA in the High Court?

Case: Delhi Development Authority vs. Diwan Chand Anand & Ors.
Date: 11th July 2022

Q: What is the significance of the Supreme Court's decision in this case?
A: The significance of the Supreme Court's decision is that it clarifies the procedure for handling cases where legal representatives of deceased parties are not brought on record, ensuring that appeals are heard on merits and not dismissed on technical grounds of abatement.
Case: Delhi Development Authority vs. Diwan Chand Anand & Ors.

Q: What was the decision of the High Court of Madhya Pradesh regarding the pension of R.D. Sharma?
A: The High Court of Madhya Pradesh held that R.D. Sharma was eligible to get the benefit of Rs. 40,000/- as pension at par with other officers, as per the Indian Forests Service (Pay) Second Amendment Rules, 2008.
Case: State of Madhya Pradesh vs. R.D. Sharma & Anr.
Date: 27th January 2022

---

Q: What was the argument of the State of Madhya Pradesh against the High Court's decision?
A: The State of Madhya Pradesh argued that the amendment rules of 2008 came into force on 27th September 2008, and since R.D. Sharma retired in 2001, he could not be granted the benefit of the apex scale of Rs. 80,000/- which was meant for the upgraded post of Head of Forest Force to be filled by selection from officers holding the post of PCCF in the HAG+ scale.
Case: State of Madhya Pradesh vs. R.D. Sharma & Anr.
Date: 27th January 2022

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's observation on the application of the principle 'equal pay for equal work' in this case?
A: The Supreme Court observed that the principle of 'equal pay for equal work' was not applicable in this case as the upgradation to the apex scale was to be made by selection and not as a matter of course. Therefore, R.D. Sharma, who retired before the 2008 amendments, could not claim the apex scale as a matter of right.
Case: State of Madhya Pradesh vs. R.D. Sharma & Anr.
Date: 27th January 2022

---

Q: What was the final decision of the Supreme Court in this case?
A: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment, and restored the order of the Central Administrative Tribunal, which had dismissed R.D. Sharma's claim for the apex scale based on 'equal pay for equal work'.
Case: State of Madhya Pradesh vs. R.D. Sharma & Anr.
Date: 27th January 2022

---

Q: What precedent did the Supreme Court rely on to support its decision?
A: The Supreme Court relied on the precedent set in the case of K.S. Krishnaswamy & Ors. vs. Union of India & Anr., where it was held that the benefit of upgradation of a post cannot be extended to pensioners who retired before such upgradation.
Case: State of Madhya Pradesh vs. R.D. Sharma & Anr.
Date: 27th January 2022

Q: What was the argument of the Union of India regarding the definition of 'pay' under the Fundamental Rules?
A: The Union of India argued that the definition of 'pay' under Rule 9(21)(a)(i) of the Fundamental Rules excludes special pay, and therefore, the special pay granted to Scientists should not be included in the computation of pension.
Case: Union of India & Ors. vs. Dr. O.P. Nijhawan & Ors.
Date: 3rd January 2019

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court observe about the nature of the special pay granted to Scientists?
A: The Supreme Court observed that the special pay of Rs. 2,000 and Rs. 4,000 granted to Scientists was not in the nature of special pay as defined in Fundamental Rule 9(25), but was instead in lieu of a separate higher pay scale. Therefore, it should be included in the computation of pension.
Case: Union of India & Ors. vs. Dr. O.P. Nijhawan & Ors.
Date: 3rd January 2019

---

Q: What was the final decision of the Supreme Court in this case?
A: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals filed by the Union of India and upheld the decisions of the Central Administrative Tribunals and High Courts, directing that the special pay of Rs. 2,000 and Rs. 4,000 be included in the computation of pension.
Case: Union of India & Ors. vs. Dr. O.P. Nijhawan & Ors.
Date: 3rd January 2019

---

Q: What was the significance of the Supreme Court's decision regarding the special pay for Scientists?
A: The significance of the Supreme Court's decision is that it clarified the treatment of special pay granted in lieu of a higher pay scale and ensured that such pay is included in the computation of pension for Scientists in the DRDO, DAE, and DOS.
Case: Union of India & Ors. vs. Dr. O.P. Nijhawan & Ors.
Date: 3rd January 2019

Q: What action did the respondent-writ petitioners take after learning about the auction sale?
A: The respondent-writ petitioners filed an application on 15th July 1983 before the Certificate Officer under Section 28 of the Bihar & Orissa Public Demands Recovery Act, 1914, to set aside the sale, claiming to have deposited the required amount on 17th September 1983.
Case: Narayan Yadav (D) Thr.Lrs. vs. The State of Bihar & Ors.
Date: 25th February 2020

---

Q: What was the decision of the Certificate Officer regarding the respondent-writ petitioners' application?
A: The Certificate Officer allowed the objections of the respondent-writ petitioners and set aside the auction sale dated 15th June 1983, permitting them to deposit the amount along with a penalty by 22nd September 1983.
Case: Narayan Yadav (D) Thr.Lrs. vs. The State of Bihar & Ors.
Date: 25th February 2020

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's interpretation of Section 28 of the Bihar & Orissa Public Demands Recovery Act, 1914?
A: The Supreme Court interpreted Section 28 as requiring the deposit of the purchase money and penalty within thirty days from the date of sale for the application to set aside the sale to be valid. The Court held that the Certificate Officer did not have the authority to extend this time period.
Case: Narayan Yadav (D) Thr.Lrs. vs. The State of Bihar & Ors.
Date: 25th February 2020

---

Q: What was the final decision of the Supreme Court in this case?
A: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment, and restored the Trial Court's order, directing the Trial Court to proceed with the trial of the suit in accordance with law.
Case: Shiv Developers vs. Aksharay Developers & Ors.
Date: 31st January 2022

---

Q: How does the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 define cruelty?
A: Cruelty under Section 13(1)(ia) of the Act is conduct that inflicts such mental pain and suffering that it makes it not possible for the petitioner to live with the other party.
Case: Smt. Roopa Soni vs. Kamalnarayan Soni

---

Q: Why did the Supreme Court grant the decree of divorce in the case of Smt. Roopa Soni vs. Kamalnarayan Soni?
A: The Supreme Court granted the decree of divorce considering the long period of separation, the serious allegations made by both parties, and the fact that both had moved on with their lives, indicating the marriage was emotionally dead and beyond salvation.
Case: Smt. Roopa Soni vs. Kamalnarayan Soni

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's final ruling in the case?
A: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal filed by Garg Builders, upholding the High Court's decision to set aside the award of pendente lite interest, and directed both parties to bear their own costs.
Case: Garg Builders vs. Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited

---

Q: What was the primary legal issue in the case Rajinder Tiwari vs. Kedar Nath (Deceased) Thr. L.Rs. & Ors.?
A: The primary legal issue was whether the High Court was justified in allowing the defendant's second appeal and dismissing the plaintiff's suit for permanent injunction in relation to the suit property.
Case: Rajinder Tiwari vs. Kedar Nath (Deceased) Thr. L.Rs. & Ors.

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's decision regarding the adequacy of the trial conducted by the lower courts?
A: The Supreme Court found the trial to be unsatisfactory as the defendant was not given an adequate opportunity to file a written statement and adduce evidence. The Court decided to remand the case to the Trial Court for a fresh trial on merits.
Case: Rajinder Tiwari vs. Kedar Nath (Deceased) Thr. L.Rs. & Ors.

---

Q: What directions did the Supreme Court give for the retrial of the case?
A: The Supreme Court directed the Trial Court to allow the respondents (legal representatives of the original defendant) to file their written statement within one month, frame issues based on the pleadings, and allow the parties to adduce their evidence, including additional documents if necessary.
Case: Rajinder Tiwari vs. Kedar Nath (Deceased) Thr. L.Rs. & Ors.

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's rationale for remanding the case to the Trial Court?
A: The Supreme Court reasoned that all contesting parties must get a fair opportunity to contest the suit on merits, and decisions rendered without such opportunity are not legally sustainable, necessitating a retrial in this case.
Case: Rajinder Tiwari vs. Kedar Nath (Deceased) Thr. L.Rs. & Ors.

Q: What was the outcome of the Writ Petitions filed by the residents of Channi Himmat and Naresh Kumar?

Q: What was the Supreme Court's decision regarding the allotment of land to J.S. Luthra Academy?

Case: J.S. Luthra Academy & Another vs. State of Jammu and Kashmir & Others

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's directive regarding the payment for the land allotted to the Academy?
A: The Supreme Court directed the Academy to pay Rs. 8,00,000 per kanal for the two kanals of land allotted for free, along with interest at the rate of 6% per annum from the date of allotment until the date of payment.
Case: J.S. Luthra Academy & Another vs. State of Jammu and Kashmir & Others

---

Q: What was the rationale provided by the Supreme Court for allowing the Academy to retain the land?
A: The Supreme Court reasoned that the allotment was made in the public interest to avoid disrupting the education of hundreds of students and to ensure continuity of the school's operation, thereby justifying the deviation from the usual practice of auctioning the land.
Case: J.S. Luthra Academy & Another vs. State of Jammu and Kashmir & Others

Q: What was the primary legal issue in the case Delma Lubna Coelho vs. Edmond Clint Fernandes?
A: The primary legal issue was whether the petition filed by the wife for the transfer of the matrimonial case from Mangaluru, Karnataka to Mumbai, Maharashtra should be granted.
Case: Delma Lubna Coelho vs. Edmond Clint Fernandes

---

Q: What did Edmond Clint Fernandes argue regarding the transfer petition?
A: Edmond Clint Fernandes argued that the wife was aware of his family background, the distance was not a problem since she traveled abroad regularly, and that she misbehaved with his parents. He also stated that he made efforts to reconcile the marriage but they were unsuccessful.
Case: Delma Lubna Coelho vs. Edmond Clint Fernandes

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court address the issue of transfer petitions in matrimonial cases?
A: The Supreme Court noted that normally, leniency is shown towards wives in transfer petitions, but each case must be considered on its own merits. The Court found that Delma Lubna Coelho, being a permanent resident of Canada and capable of traveling, did not present a strong enough case for transfer.
Case: Delma Lubna Coelho vs. Edmond Clint Fernandes

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's final decision on the transfer petition?
A: The Supreme Court dismissed the transfer petition, stating that Delma Lubna Coelho could attend the hearings in Mangaluru and seek exemption from appearance whenever required. The Court did not find sufficient grounds to transfer the case to Mumbai.
Case: Delma Lubna Coelho vs. Edmond Clint Fernandes

---

Q: Did the Supreme Court grant any relief regarding travel expenses for Delma Lubna Coelho?
A: The Supreme Court did not initially grant any relief regarding travel expenses but allowed Delma Lubna Coelho to file an application for reimbursement of expenses before the concerned court, which would be examined on its own merits.
Case: Delma Lubna Coelho vs. Edmond Clint Fernandes

Q: What was the accident that led to the filing of the claim petition by M.H. Uma Maheshwari & Ors.?

Case: M.H. Uma Maheshwari & Ors. vs. United India Insurance Co. Ltd. & Anr.

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's view on the High Court's adjustment of future prospects?
A: The Supreme Court held that the High Court erred in reducing future prospects to 15% because the age group of the deceased was considered to be between 40 to 50 years, which warrants a 30% addition for future prospects as per established legal precedents.
Case: M.H. Uma Maheshwari & Ors. vs. United India Insurance Co. Ltd. & Anr.

Q: What considerations did the Supreme Court take into account for the transfer decision?
A: The Supreme Court considered the convenience of the wife, the economic soundness, social strata, and the practical difficulties she would face in traveling to Vellore, along with the desirability of clubbing all related proceedings in one jurisdiction.
Case: N.C.V. Aishwarya vs. A.S. Saravana Karthik Sha

Q: How did the High Court of Calcutta rule on the Trust's appeal?

Q: What was the Supreme Court's decision regarding the High Court's ruling?

Q: What directions did the Supreme Court give for the reconsideration of the case?
A: The Supreme Court directed the Commissioner of Income Tax (Exemptions), Kolkata to reconsider the case on its own merits, without being influenced by the observations of the appellate authority, the High Court, or the Supreme Court in this order.

Q: What was the Supreme Court's final decision in the case?

---

Q: What were the substantial questions of law framed by the High Court in Radha Bai vs Ram Narayan & Ors.?
A: The substantial questions of law were: 1) Whether Radha Bai, being a female, had the right to partition the property that belonged to Sukhdeo and devolved upon Janak Ram by survivorship. 2) Whether the suit land inherited by Janak Ram from Sukhdeo became ancestral property for Radha Bai on the date of Sukhdeo's death and Janak Ram's death.
Case: Radha Bai vs Ram Narayan & Ors.

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's decision in the case of Radha Bai vs Ram Narayan & Ors.?
A: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal filed by Radha Bai, upholding the High Court's decision that the property devolved upon Janakram and Pilaram equally after Sukhdeo's death, and the appellant Radha Bai had no claim to it.
Case: Radha Bai vs Ram Narayan & Ors.

---

Q: Why did the Supreme Court reject Radha Bai's claim in the case against Ram Narayan & Ors.?
A: The Supreme Court rejected Radha Bai's claim because her father Saheblal predeceased his father Janakram and grandfather Sukhdeo, meaning he could not have succeeded to the property. Consequently, Radha Bai, being his daughter, could not claim a higher right than her father.
Case: Radha Bai vs Ram Narayan & Ors.

---

Q: What legal principles did the Supreme Court apply in the case of Radha Bai vs Ram Narayan & Ors.?
A: The Supreme Court applied the principles of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, specifically Section 6, which deals with devolution of interest in coparcenary property and the rule of survivorship.
Case: Radha Bai vs Ram Narayan & Ors.

---

Q: What were the two main points raised by the appellant Bank of Baroda against the High Court's decision?
A: The appellant Bank argued that Baljit Singh did not meet the financial eligibility criteria and that the High Court failed to consider the factual aspects of the case properly.
Case: Bank of Baroda & Ors. vs. Baljit Singh

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court rule regarding the financial eligibility of Baljit Singh for compassionate appointment?
A: The Supreme Court ruled that Baljit Singh did not meet the financial eligibility criteria as the family's monthly income exceeded 60% of the deceased employee's last drawn emoluments, thus disqualifying him from compassionate appointment under the Scheme.
Case: Bank of Baroda & Ors. vs. Baljit Singh

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court address the issue of the respondent's educational qualifications?
A: The Supreme Court acknowledged that Baljit Singh had completed the 8th standard during his father's lifetime and was therefore eligible for the post of Peon, but this did not affect his ineligibility based on the family's financial status.
Case: Bank of Baroda & Ors. vs. Baljit Singh

---

Q: What was the final decision of the Supreme Court in the case?
A: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment, and dismissed Baljit Singh's suit for compassionate appointment.
Case: Bank of Baroda & Ors. vs. Baljit Singh

---

Q: What was the decision of the High Court regarding the levy of gallonage fee, licence fee, and shop rental (kist) on FL-9 licences?
A: The High Court held that the levy of gallonage fee, licence fee, and shop rental (kist) with respect to FL-9 licences granted to the appellant falls within the purview of Section 40(a)(iib) and the amount paid in this regard is liable to be disallowed.
Case: Kerala State Beverages Manufacturing & Marketing Corporation Ltd. v. The Assistant Commissioner of Income Tax Circle 1(1)

---

Q: How did the High Court rule on the surcharge on sales tax and turnover tax?
A: The High Court ruled that the surcharge on sales tax and turnover tax is not a 'fee or charge' within the meaning of Section 40(a)(iib) and therefore cannot be disallowed under this provision.
Case: Kerala State Beverages Manufacturing & Marketing Corporation Ltd. v. The Assistant Commissioner of Income Tax Circle 1(1)

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court state about the interpretation of Section 40(a)(iib) regarding exclusivity?
A: The Supreme Court stated that the interpretation of Section 40(a)(iib) should be viewed from the nature of the undertaking on which the levy is imposed, not on the number of undertakings. This means that the levy of gallonage fee, licence fee, and shop rental (kist) is an exclusive levy on the State Government Undertakings and should be disallowed.
Case: Kerala State Beverages Manufacturing & Marketing Corporation Ltd. v. The Assistant Commissioner of Income Tax Circle 1(1)

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court view the surcharge on sales tax in relation to Section 40(a)(iib)?
A: The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court that the surcharge on sales tax is a tax and not a 'fee' or 'charge'. Therefore, it is outside the scope of Section 40(a)(iib)(A) and (B) of the Income-tax Act and should not be disallowed.
Case: Kerala State Beverages Manufacturing & Marketing Corporation Ltd. v. The Assistant Commissioner of Income Tax Circle 1(1)

---

Q: What was the decision of the Central Administrative Tribunal, Patna, and the High Court of Patna in this case?

Case: Mukesh Kumar & Anr. vs. The Union of India & Ors.

Q: What argument did the counsel for the appellants present in support of their claim?
A: The counsel for the appellants argued that the issue was covered by the Supreme Court's decision in Union of India v. V.R. Tripathi, which held that a child of a second wife of an employee could not be denied compassionate appointment on that ground alone.
Case: Mukesh Kumar & Anr. vs. The Union of India & Ors.

Q: How did the Supreme Court address the issue of discrimination in this case?
A: The Supreme Court held that denying compassionate appointment to children of a second wife solely on that ground is discriminatory and violates Article 16(2) of the Constitution, which prohibits discrimination based on descent.
Case: Mukesh Kumar & Anr. vs. The Union of India & Ors.

Q: What was the Supreme Court's final decision in the case Mukesh Kumar & Anr. vs. The Union of India & Ors.?

Q: What previous cases did the Supreme Court refer to in its judgment?
A: The Supreme Court referred to its own decision in Union of India v. V.R. Tripathi and the decisions of the High Courts in cases like Namita Goldar v. Union of India and Union of India v. Pankaj Kumar Sharma, which held similar views on compassionate appointments for children of second marriages.

Q: What was the High Court's decision regarding Narendra Kumar's pensionary benefits?

Case: Narendra Kumar vs. Chairman and Managing Director, Syndicate Bank & Ors.

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's view on the technicality of Narendra Kumar's service interruption?
A: The Supreme Court viewed the bank's stance as hyper-technical and unjustified, noting that Narendra Kumar had obtained a 'No Objection Certificate' from the bank and had written a letter to the bank for permission to take over the new post, which elicited no response for 11 months.
Case: Narendra Kumar vs. Chairman and Managing Director, Syndicate Bank & Ors.

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court conclude about the interruption in Narendra Kumar's service?
A: The Supreme Court concluded that there was no interruption in service, as Narendra Kumar's deputation and subsequent appointment were part of his continuous service. The bank's refusal to grant pensionary benefits was deemed inappropriate and unjustified.
Case: Narendra Kumar vs. Chairman and Managing Director, Syndicate Bank & Ors.

---

Q: What relief did the Supreme Court grant to Narendra Kumar?
A: The Supreme Court quashed the impugned orders of the bank and the High Court, allowing Narendra Kumar's writ petition and directing the bank to grant him pensionary benefits along with interest and imposing costs of Rs. 25,000 on the bank.
Case: Narendra Kumar vs. Chairman and Managing Director, Syndicate Bank & Ors.

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court view the Tribunal's decision in this case?
A: The Supreme Court upheld the Tribunal's decision, agreeing that the declared transaction value should be accepted unless cogent reasons are provided to reject it, and that the Assessing Officer failed to provide such reasons.
Case: Commissioner of Central Excise and Service Tax, Noida vs. M/S. Sanjivani Non-Ferrous Trading Pvt. Ltd.

Q: What legal principles did the Supreme Court emphasize in its judgment?

Case: Commissioner of Central Excise and Service Tax, Noida vs. M/S. Sanjivani Non-Ferrous Trading Pvt. Ltd.

Q: What did the Division Bench of the Delhi High Court rule regarding the applicability of Section 213 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925?
A: The Division Bench of the Delhi High Court held that the bar under Section 213 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 is not applicable and set aside the order of rejection of plaint, directing that both the suits be clubbed and common evidence be led together.
Case: Kanta Yadav vs. Om Prakash Yadav & Ors.

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's interpretation of Section 213 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 in this case?
A: The Supreme Court interpreted that Section 213 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 requires probate or letter of administration only for Wills made within the territories of Bengal, Madras, or Bombay, or for immovable properties situated within those territories, and is not applicable to Delhi.
Case: Kanta Yadav vs. Om Prakash Yadav & Ors.

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's view on the need for probate in Delhi for Wills made by Hindus, Buddhists, Sikhs, or Jains?
A: The Supreme Court held that it is not necessary to seek probate or letter of administration for Wills made by Hindus, Buddhists, Sikhs, or Jains in Delhi, as Delhi is not covered by the territories mentioned in Section 57(a) and (b) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925.
Case: Kanta Yadav vs. Om Prakash Yadav & Ors.

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's final decision in the case of Kanta Yadav vs. Om Prakash Yadav & Ors.?
A: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the Division Bench's judgment that Section 213 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 is not applicable to the National Capital Region of Delhi, and both suits should proceed with common evidence.
Case: Kanta Yadav vs. Om Prakash Yadav & Ors.

Date: 8th December 2020

---

Q: What was the main legal issue in the case of The State of Haryana vs. Ashok Khemka & Anr.?
A: The main legal issue was whether the High Court of Punjab and Haryana correctly set aside the order of the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT), which had rejected Ashok Khemka's performance appraisal report (PAR) for the period 2016-2017.
Case: The State of Haryana vs. Ashok Khemka & Anr.

---

Q: What was the High Court's decision regarding Ashok Khemka's performance appraisal report (PAR)?
A: The High Court set aside the CAT's order, expunged the opinion of the Accepting Authority, and restored the opinion and grade awarded by the Reviewing Authority, which was 9.92.
Case: The State of Haryana vs. Ashok Khemka & Anr.

---

Q: What were the main reasons provided by the High Court for setting aside the CAT's order?
A: The High Court noted that the Accepting Authority failed to appreciate the practical constraints faced by Ashok Khemka, and that the Reviewing Authority had revised the grade in a transparent, fair, and reasoned manner.
Case: The State of Haryana vs. Ashok Khemka & Anr.

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court decide regarding the timelines prescribed under the PAR Rules?
A: The Supreme Court found that although the Accepting Authority recorded remarks after the prescribed timeline, it was within the mandatory timeline under Rule 5(1) of the PAR Rules, and therefore, the remarks and grade should not be expunged.
Case: The State of Haryana vs. Ashok Khemka & Anr.

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's view on the High Court's interference with the CAT's order?
A: The Supreme Court held that the High Court overstepped its jurisdiction by interfering with the CAT's order, as it entered a specialized domain of evaluating an IAS officer's competency without the requisite expertise.
Case: The State of Haryana vs. Ashok Khemka & Anr.

---

Q: What direction did the Supreme Court give regarding the pending decision on Ashok Khemka's representation?
A: The Supreme Court directed the Accepting Authority to take a decision on Ashok Khemka's representation under Rule 9(7B) of the PAR Rules within 60 days from the date of the judgment.
Case: The State of Haryana vs. Ashok Khemka & Anr.

---

Q: What was the final outcome of the Supreme Court's judgment in The State of Haryana vs. Ashok Khemka & Anr.?
A: The Supreme Court set aside the judgment of the Division Bench of the High Court, directed the Accepting Authority to decide on the pending representation, and allowed the appeal filed by the State of Haryana.
Case: The State of Haryana vs. Ashok Khemka & Anr.

---

Q: What did the Division Bench of the High Court decide regarding Premlata's appointment?
A: The Division Bench of the High Court set aside the Single Judge's order and directed the appellants to consider Premlata's candidature for a Grade-III post on compassionate grounds.
Case: The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors. vs. Premlata

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's interpretation of 'suitable post' under Rule 5 of the Dying-in-Harness Rules 1974?
A: The Supreme Court interpreted 'suitable post' as one that should be considered in relation to the post held by the deceased employee, not just based on the qualifications of the candidate. The court emphasized that the post offered should align with the deceased employee's position to maintain the compassionate appointment's purpose.
Case: The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors. vs. Premlata

---

Q: What was the final decision of the Supreme Court in the case of The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors. vs. Premlata?
A: The Supreme Court quashed the Division Bench's decision and restored the Single Judge's order, dismissing Premlata's writ petition and upholding the decision to offer her the post of Messenger.
Case: The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors. vs. Premlata

---

Q: What did the petitioners contend regarding the implementation of the OROP policy?
A: The petitioners contended that the principle of OROP was replaced by 'one rank multiple pensions' and that the revision from automatic updates to periodic intervals was arbitrary and unconstitutional under Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution.
Case: Indian Ex Servicemen Movement & Ors. vs Union of India & Ors.
Date: 16th March 2022

---

Q: What was the original definition of OROP as discussed by the petitioners?
A: The original definition of OROP was the payment of uniform pension to armed services personnel retiring in the same rank with the same length of service, irrespective of the date of retirement, with automatic revision of pension rates in case of future enhancements.
Case: Indian Ex Servicemen Movement & Ors. vs Union of India & Ors.
Date: 16th March 2022

---

Q: What was the outcome of the case regarding the implementation of the revised OROP policy?
A: The outcome of the case was that the Supreme Court of India upheld the revised definition of OROP as implemented by the Union Government, noting that the policy was a matter of executive decision and not open to judicial review on the grounds of being contrary to the original intent.
Case: Indian Ex Servicemen Movement & Ors. vs Union of India & Ors.
Date: 16th March 2022

---

Q: What were the petitioners' arguments against the OBC and EWS reservations in AIQ seats?
A: The petitioners argued that there should be no reservation for the OBC and EWS categories in AIQ seats in NEET-PG and that the criteria for determining the EWS category, specifically the Rs. 8 lakhs income limit, were unconstitutional.
Case: Neil Aurelio Nunes & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors.

A: The Union Government formed a committee on 30th November 2021 to review the criteria for identifying EWS. Case: Neil Aurelio Nunes & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors.

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's interim order regarding the implementation of the OBC and EWS reservations for NEET-PG 2021 and NEET-UG 2021?
A: The Supreme Court ordered that the OBC and EWS reservations as per the notice dated 29th July 2021 be implemented for the current admission year, and the criteria specified in the OM 2019 be used for identifying the EWS category.
Case: Neil Aurelio Nunes & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors.

Q: What future actions did the Supreme Court direct regarding the EWS criteria?
A: The Supreme Court directed that the criteria for determining the EWS, as recommended by the Pandey Committee, would be subject to the final outcome of the petitions, which were scheduled for a final hearing in the third week of March 2022.
Case: Neil Aurelio Nunes & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors.

Q: What was the Supreme Court's decision regarding the interim relief sought by Tamil Nadu?

Q: What was the stance of the Supreme Court regarding the interpretation of the word 'entertain' in Section 9(3) of the Arbitration Act?
A: The Supreme Court held that the word 'entertain' in Section 9(3) means the entire process up to its final adjudication and passing of an order on merits. Therefore, if the application is already entertained and arguments are heard, the Court can proceed to pass an order even after the Arbitral Tribunal is constituted.

Q: What is the main reason for the Supreme Court to exercise its contempt jurisdiction in this case?
A: The Supreme Court exercised its contempt jurisdiction to maintain the dignity of judicial forums and to address the persistent and inappropriate conduct of the petitioner, Mr. Rajiv Daiya, who sought to justify his existence by making disparaging statements against the judiciary.
Case: Suraz India Trust vs. Union of India

---

Q: What was the outcome of the original judgment dated 1st May 2017 in Writ Petition (C) No.880 of 2016?
A: The original judgment found the litigation initiated by Suraz India Trust to be thoughtless and frivolous. It barred the Trust and its Chairman, Mr. Rajiv Daiya, from filing any public interest petitions in any court and imposed exemplary costs of Rs. 25 lakhs on Mr. Daiya.
Case: Suraz India Trust vs. Union of India

---

Q: What actions did Mr. Rajiv Daiya take that led to the contempt proceedings against him?
A: Mr. Rajiv Daiya sent disparaging communications to the residential offices of Hon'ble Judges, made representations to the President and Prime Minister, and continued to file frivolous petitions despite being barred. He also failed to deposit the imposed costs and attempted to scandalize the court through various communications.
Case: Suraz India Trust vs. Union of India

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's decision regarding Mr. Rajiv Daiya's request for an unconditional apology and waiver of costs?
A: The Supreme Court found Mr. Daiya's apology insincere and noted that he continued to make allegations against the judiciary. The Court closed Miscellaneous Application No.1630/2020 by directing the State Government to commence the process of recovering costs as 'arrears of land revenue'.
Case: Suraz India Trust vs. Union of India

---

Q: What are the implications of the Supreme Court's decision for Mr. Rajiv Daiya and Suraz India Trust?
A: The decision implies that Mr. Rajiv Daiya and Suraz India Trust are barred from filing public interest petitions and must face the consequences of their actions, including the recovery of imposed costs. The Court's decision underscores the importance of maintaining the dignity of the judiciary and holding litigants accountable for frivolous and scandalous conduct.
Case: Suraz India Trust vs. Union of India

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's observation regarding the need for judicial intervention in cases of persistent contemptuous conduct?
A: The Supreme Court observed that persistent contemptuous conduct by litigants must be addressed to uphold the dignity and majesty of the law. The Court emphasized that it is the duty of judges to perform their tasks for the larger good of the institution, even when faced with challenging and scandalous behavior from litigants like Mr. Rajiv Daiya.
Case: Suraz India Trust vs. Union of India

Q: What was the primary objective of the writ petition filed by M.K. Ranjitsinh & Ors. against the Union of India & Ors.?
A: The primary objective was to seek protection for two species of birds, the Great Indian Bustard and the Lesser Florican, which are on the verge of extinction due to hazards posed by overhead power lines.
Case: M.K. Ranjitsinh & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors.
Date: 19th April 2021

---

Q: What interim directions were sought in the application filed by the petitioners in this case?
A: The petitioners sought interim directions to ensure predator-proof fencing, controlled grazing, to prevent the installation of overhead power lines, and to stop further construction of windmills and solar infrastructure in the habitats of the endangered birds.
Case: M.K. Ranjitsinh & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors.
Date: 19th April 2021

---

Q: What measures did the Supreme Court suggest to mitigate the threat posed by power lines to the Great Indian Bustard?
A: The Supreme Court suggested installing bird divertors on existing power lines and laying new power lines underground wherever technically feasible, especially in the habitats of the Great Indian Bustard.
Case: M.K. Ranjitsinh & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors.
Date: 19th April 2021

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court say about the responsibility of the State and Central Government regarding the conservation of endangered species?
A: The Supreme Court stated that both the State and Central Government have a duty to preserve endangered species and should provide the necessary funds for conservation efforts, including the undergrounding of power lines in the habitats of the Great Indian Bustard.
Case: M.K. Ranjitsinh & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors.
Date: 19th April 2021

---

Q: What was the role of the committee constituted by the Supreme Court in this case?
A: The committee was tasked with assessing the feasibility of laying underground power lines in the habitats of the Great Indian Bustard and to provide technical evaluations on a case-by-case basis.
Case: M.K. Ranjitsinh & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors.
Date: 19th April 2021

---

Q: What specific directions did the Supreme Court give regarding the existing and future power lines in the habitats of the Great Indian Bustard?
A: The Supreme Court directed that all existing low voltage power lines in the priority and potential habitats of the Great Indian Bustard be converted to underground lines, and that future power lines should be laid underground wherever feasible. Bird divertors should be installed on all existing overhead lines.
Case: M.K. Ranjitsinh & Ors. vs. Union of India & Ors.
Date: 19th April 2021

Q: What did the Supreme Court decide regarding the calculation of Kajal's loss of future earnings?
A: The Supreme Court held that the notional income of Rs.15,000 per annum taken by the lower courts was not justified. Instead, they considered the minimum wages for a skilled workman, which with future prospects amounted to Rs.81,412.80 per annum. Using a multiplier of 18, the total was Rs.14,66,000.
Case: Kajal vs. Jagdish Chand & Ors.
Date: 5th February 2020

Q: How did the Supreme Court address the future medical treatment costs for Kajal?
A: The Supreme Court awarded Rs.5,00,000 for future medical expenses, considering her severe and lifelong medical needs.
Case: Kajal vs. Jagdish Chand & Ors.
Date: 5th February 2020

Q: What did the Full Bench of the High Court conclude regarding the stay orders affecting the period for publication of the notification under Section 6?

Q: What was the High Court's reasoning in setting aside the Section 6 notification in the Balak Ram Gupta case?
A: The High Court set aside the Section 6 notification in the Balak Ram Gupta case because the writ petitioner was neither given an opportunity of personal hearing nor actually heard in the objections filed under Section 5A. There was no record maintained for consideration of the objections, and it was deemed that the writ petitioner's right to know the reasons for declining exemption was violated.
Case: Delhi Development Authority vs Sunil Khatri & Ors.

Q: What was the landowners' argument regarding the stay orders and the five-year period before the 2013 Act?
A: The landowners argued that the period of stay granted in writ petitions filed by other landowners should not be excluded for the purposes of Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act. They contended that since the award was announced in 1987 and the interim stay order was passed in 1999, there was a 12-year period without any stay, thus the acquisition proceedings should lapse.
Case: Delhi Development Authority vs Sunil Khatri & Ors.

Q: What was the Supreme Court's decision in this appeal regarding the applicability of Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act?
A: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's order, and held that the acquisition proceedings had not lapsed under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act because the period of five years had not expired free from stay or quashing of notifications. The interim orders and the legal uncertainty prevented the appellant from taking possession within the required time frame.
Case: Delhi Development Authority vs Sunil Khatri & Ors.
