Date: 4th May 2022

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's interpretation of the term 'approval' in the exemption notification?
A: The Supreme Court interpreted the term 'approval' to mean the unambiguous approval by the Central Government, which in this case was granted on 27th October 1994, when the 'Green Card' was issued, rather than the initial permission letter dated 16th December 1993.
Case: State of Kerala vs. M/S Akay Flavours and Aromatics Ltd.
Date: 2nd February 2023

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's final decision regarding the commencement of the exemption period?
A: The Supreme Court held that the exemption period should commence from the date of final approval by the Central Government, which was 27th October 1994. The appeals were partly allowed, and the date of approval was set as the reckonable date for the grant of exemption under the notification SRO 1727/1993.
Case: State of Kerala vs. M/S Akay Flavours and Aromatics Ltd.
Date: 2nd February 2023

---

Q: What was the primary challenge in the writ petition filed by Haji Abdul Gani Khan & Anr. against the Union of India & Ors.?
A: The primary challenge was to the legality and validity of constituting a Delimitation Commission for the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir under the provisions of the Delimitation Act, 2002 and the exercise of delimitation undertaken by the Commission.
Case: Haji Abdul Gani Khan & Anr. vs. Union of India & Ors.
Date: 13th February 2023

---

Q: What were the main provisions of the Constitution (Application to Jammu and Kashmir) Order, 2019 issued on 5th August 2019?
A: The order directed that all the provisions of the Constitution of India, as amended from time to time, shall apply in relation to the State of Jammu and Kashmir, subject to modifications made to Article 367. Clause (4) was added to Article 367, providing that the expression 'Constituent Assembly of the State referred to in clause (2)' in the proviso to clause (3) of Article 370 shall be read as 'Legislative Assembly of the State'.
Case: Haji Abdul Gani Khan & Anr. vs. Union of India & Ors.
Date: 13th February 2023

---

Q: On what grounds did the petitioners challenge the constitution of the Delimitation Commission?
A: The petitioners challenged the constitution of the Delimitation Commission on the grounds that it was appointed by usurping the jurisdiction of the Election Commission of India and was thus ultra vires the provisions of sub-sections (2) and (5) of Section 60 of the J&K Reorganisation Act. They also contended that it infringed clause (3) of Article 170 as well as Articles 14, 19, and 21 of the Constitution.
Case: Haji Abdul Gani Khan & Anr. vs. Union of India & Ors.
Date: 13th February 2023

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's stance on the validity of the J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019?
A: The Supreme Court noted that there was no specific challenge to the constitutional validity of the provisions of the J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019 in the writ petition. Therefore, the Court proceeded on the footing that the 2019 Presidential Order, the said declaration, and the provisions of the J&K Reorganisation Act are valid.
Case: Haji Abdul Gani Khan & Anr. vs. Union of India & Ors.
Date: 13th February 2023

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's interpretation of the applicability of Article 170 to the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir?
A: The Supreme Court concluded that Article 170, which deals with the composition of the Legislative Assemblies, forms part of Chapter III of Part VI of the Constitution and deals only with the State Legislature. Therefore, it has no application to the Legislatures of Union Territories, including the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir.
Case: Haji Abdul Gani Khan & Anr. vs. Union of India & Ors.
Date: 13th February 2023

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court decide regarding the delimitation exercise conducted by the Delimitation Commission for the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir?
A: The Supreme Court held that there was nothing illegal about the delimitation exercise conducted by the Delimitation Commission for dividing the Union Territory into 90 constituencies on the basis of the 2011 census figures, as mandated by sub-sections (2) and (3) of Section 62 of the J&K Reorganisation Act.
Case: Haji Abdul Gani Khan & Anr. vs. Union of India & Ors.
Date: 13th February 2023

---

Q: What was the ruling of the Kerala High Court regarding the 2014 amendments to the Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995?
A: The Kerala High Court ruled that the 2014 amendments to the Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995 were invalid. The court held that the amendments were arbitrary, especially the capping of the salary at Rs. 15,000 for pension calculations and the requirement for employees to contribute an additional 1.16% on salaries exceeding Rs. 15,000. The court found that these amendments deprived employees of benefits without any justification.
Case: The Employees Provident Fund Organisation & Anr. etc. vs. Sunil Kumar B. & Ors. etc.
Date: 4th November 2022

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court of India respond to the appeals against the High Court judgements regarding the 2014 amendments?
A: The Supreme Court of India allowed the appeals against the High Court judgements, thereby upholding the legality of the 2014 amendments to the Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995. The court acknowledged the financial implications of the scheme and the need for sustainable pension funding, agreeing with the Central Government's amendments.
Case: The Employees Provident Fund Organisation & Anr. etc. vs. Sunil Kumar B. & Ors. etc.
Date: 4th November 2022

---

Q: What is the significance of the judgement in the case of R.C. Gupta and Others vs. Regional Provident Fund Commissioner in relation to the Employees’ Pension Scheme?
A: The judgement in the case of R.C. Gupta and Others vs. Regional Provident Fund Commissioner was significant as it addressed the issue of entitlement of members whose pensionable salary exceeded the ceiling limit to exercise an option under the proviso to paragraph 11(3) of the scheme. The Supreme Court held that the dates specified in clause 11(3) were not cut-off dates and that a beneficial scheme should not be defeated by a cut-off date, especially when employers had contributed based on actual salaries.
Case: The Employees Provident Fund Organisation & Anr. etc. vs. Sunil Kumar B. & Ors. etc.
Date: 4th November 2022

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's final decision regarding the 2014 amendments to the Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995?
A: The Supreme Court's final decision was to uphold the 2014 amendments to the Employees' Pension Scheme, 1995. The court recognized the financial sustainability concerns raised by the Central Government and found that the amendments were necessary to ensure the continued viability of the pension scheme.
Case: The Employees Provident Fund Organisation & Anr. etc. vs. Sunil Kumar B. & Ors. etc.
Date: 4th November 2022

---

Q: What was the High Court's decision regarding Ashish Kumar's eligibility?
A: The High Court dismissed Ashish Kumar's appeal, agreeing with the respondents that the qualification required was both a graduate degree in Psychology and a training qualification like L.T./B.T.B.Ed.
Case: Ashish Kumar vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.
Date: 31st January 2018

---

Q: What interpretation did the Supreme Court provide regarding the advertisement for the 'Psychologist' post?
A: The Supreme Court interpreted the advertisement to mean that the qualifications of graduation in Psychology, L.T./B.T.B.Ed., were alternative and not cumulative. Therefore, Ashish Kumar was eligible with his qualifications.
Case: Ashish Kumar vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.
Date: 31st January 2018

---

Q: What was the final decision of the Supreme Court in Ashish Kumar's case?
A: The Supreme Court set aside the judgements of the High Court and directed the respondents to issue an appointment order to Ashish Kumar for the post of 'Psychologist' within two months.
Case: Ashish Kumar vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.
Date: 31st January 2018

---

Q: What were the key contentions raised by the appellants in the Supreme Court?
A: The appellants contended that the High Court and the Tribunal failed to consider the deceased's Income Tax Return, did not account for the higher number of dependents, and did not award the appropriate amounts under conventional heads and for future prospects.
Case: Smt. Anjali & Ors. vs. Lokendra Rathod & Ors.
Date: 6th December 2022

---

Q: What did the High Court rule regarding the +2 lecturers appointed pursuant to Advertisement No. 1/87?
A: The High Court ruled that the +2 lecturers appointed pursuant to Advertisement No. 1/87 were always part of the Bihar Subordinate Education Service (BSES) and therefore entitled to be merged with the Bihar Education Service (BES), quashing the notification dated 23rd June 2009 which contradicted this decision.
Case: State of Bihar & Ors. vs. Shyama Nandan Mishra
Date: 5th May 2022

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's stance on the Bihar Government's fluctuating decisions regarding the +2 lecturers?
A: The Supreme Court noted the Bihar Government's fluctuating and indecisive stance, which led to repeated litigations. The Court criticized the government's attempts to circumvent its earlier decisions and the High Court's decision, emphasizing that the +2 lecturers should be treated as part of the BSES.
Case: State of Bihar & Ors. vs. Shyama Nandan Mishra
Date: 5th May 2022

---

Q: What was the final decision of the Supreme Court in the case of State of Bihar & Ors. vs. Shyama Nandan Mishra?
A: The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, stating that the +2 lecturers appointed under Advertisement No. 1/87 are members of the Subordinate Educational Service and should receive all service benefits as such, dismissing the appeals and granting the state six months to comply with the High Court's directions.
Case: State of Bihar & Ors. vs. Shyama Nandan Mishra
Date: 5th May 2022

---

Q: Why did the Supreme Court find the Bihar Government's action of issuing the notification dated 23rd June 2009 problematic?
A: The Supreme Court found the notification dated 23rd June 2009 problematic because it encadred +2 lecturers with nationalized secondary school teachers, which was contrary to the legitimate expectations created by the 1985 notification and the 1987 advertisement, thereby denying the +2 lecturers promotional opportunities and fair treatment.
Case: State of Bihar & Ors. vs. Shyama Nandan Mishra
Date: 5th May 2022

---

Q: What was the High Court of Delhi's decision regarding the land acquisition proceedings?
A: The High Court of Delhi declared that the land acquisition proceedings initiated under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, were deemed to have lapsed under Section 24(2) of the Act, 2013.
Case: Government of NCT of Delhi & Anr. vs. Shakeel Ahmed & Ors.
Date: 9th February 2023

---

Q: What was the basis for the High Court's decision in this case?
A: The High Court's decision was based on the precedent set by the case of Pune Municipal Corporation and Anr. vs. Harakchand Misirimal Solanki and Ors., which was subsequently overruled by the Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court in Indore Development Authority vs. Manoharlal and Ors.
Case: Government of NCT of Delhi & Anr. vs. Shakeel Ahmed & Ors.
Date: 9th February 2023

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's final decision in the case?
A: The Supreme Court quashed the High Court's judgement and order, ruling that the land acquisition proceedings had not lapsed under Section 24(2) of the Act, 2013, and restored the validity of the land acquisition proceedings initiated under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Case: Government of NCT of Delhi & Anr. vs. Shakeel Ahmed & Ors.
Date: 9th February 2023

---

Q: What was the ruling of the Division Bench of the High Court regarding the use of the trade mark 'Prius'?
A: The Division Bench of the High Court set aside the trial court's order, holding that the plaintiff had not established sufficient goodwill and reputation of the 'Prius' mark in the Indian market prior to the defendants' use of the mark in 2001. The court found that the plaintiff had delayed in asserting its rights in India.
Case: Toyota Jidosha Kabushiki Kaisha vs. M/S Prius Auto Industries Ltd. & Ors.

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court rule on the applicability of the ten-year cap for Mahabir Industries?
A: The Supreme Court ruled that the ten-year cap under Section 80-IC(6) should not include the years for which deductions were claimed under Section 80-IA, as this provision applied specifically to industries in the North-Eastern Region, which was not the case for Mahabir Industries.
Case: Mahabir Industries vs. Principal Commissioner of Income Tax
Date: 18th May 2018

---

Q: What was the final outcome of the Supreme Court's decision for Mahabir Industries?
A: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgement and allowed Mahabir Industries to claim deductions under Section 80-IC for the Assessment Years 2008-09 and 2009-10, recognizing the substantial expansion completed in the Assessment Year 2006-07.
Case: Mahabir Industries vs. Principal Commissioner of Income Tax
Date: 18th May 2018

---

Q: What did the High Court of Punjab and Haryana decide regarding the promotions of respondent nos. 2 and 3?
A: The High Court of Punjab and Haryana reversed the promotions of respondent nos. 2 and 3, ruling that their promotions were in violation of the statutory rules as they had not performed the duties of a Section Officer on an independent basis.

Q: How did the High Court of Orissa rule on the appeal by the Union Public Service Commission?

Q: How did the Supreme Court interpret the term 'primarily leviable' in Clause 6 of the lease deed?
A: The Supreme Court interpreted the term 'primarily leviable' to mean that the person liable for paying the tax is the service provider, i.e., the lessor, and not the recipient of the service, i.e., the lessee.
Case: Union of India & Ors. vs. Bengal Shrachi Housing Development Limited & Anr.

---

Q: What was the main issue in the case of Ratanlal @ Babulal Chunilal Samsuka vs. Sundarabai Govardhandas Samsuka (D.) Th. LRS. & Ors.?
A: The main issue was whether Ratanlal was the legally adopted son of late Govardhandas Laxmichand Samsuka, which would entitle him to represent himself as Govardhandas's son and claim rights to his estate.
Case: Ratanlal @ Babulal Chunilal Samsuka vs. Sundarabai Govardhandas Samsuka (D.) Th. LRS. & Ors.
Date: 22nd November 2017

---

Q: What was the judgement of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay regarding Ratanlal's adoption?
A: The High Court of Judicature at Bombay declared that Ratanlal was not the adopted son of late Govardhandas and consequently restrained him from representing himself as Govardhandas's son or using the name Ratanlal Govardhandas Samsuka.
Case: Ratanlal @ Babulal Chunilal Samsuka vs. Sundarabai Govardhandas Samsuka (D.) Th. LRS. & Ors.
Date: 22nd November 2017

---

Q: What were the key findings of the High Court that led to the rejection of Ratanlal's adoption claim?
A: The High Court found several issues: non-production of negatives of adoption photographs, lack of proof of any ceremony in the photographs, contradictions in testimonies regarding the adoption, and continuous use of Ratanlal's biological father's name post-adoption.
Case: Ratanlal @ Babulal Chunilal Samsuka vs. Sundarabai Govardhandas Samsuka (D.) Th. LRS. & Ors.
Date: 22nd November 2017

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's stance on the High Court's judgement?
A: The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's judgement, agreeing that Ratanlal failed to prove the factum of adoption with cogent evidence and noting suspicious circumstances that were not satisfactorily explained.
Case: Ratanlal @ Babulal Chunilal Samsuka vs. Sundarabai Govardhandas Samsuka (D.) Th. LRS. & Ors.
Date: 22nd November 2017

---

Q: What legal principle did the Supreme Court emphasize regarding the burden of proving adoption?
A: The Supreme Court emphasized that the burden of proving adoption is heavy and requires clear, consistent, and convincing evidence, particularly when the adoption changes the course of succession and affects property rights.
Case: Ratanlal @ Babulal Chunilal Samsuka vs. Sundarabai Govardhandas Samsuka (D.) Th. LRS. & Ors.
Date: 22nd November 2017

---

Q: What was the final outcome of the Supreme Court's decision in this case?
A: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, maintaining that Ratanlal's claim of adoption was not proven and upholding the High Court's ruling that he is not the adopted son of Govardhandas.
Case: Ratanlal @ Babulal Chunilal Samsuka vs. Sundarabai Govardhandas Samsuka (D.) Th. LRS. & Ors.
Date: 22nd November 2017

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's reasoning behind allowing the appeal?
A: The Supreme Court reasoned that the Pollution Control Board had followed due process by issuing show cause notices and conducting hearings. It found that the bank guarantees were invoked in terms of the conditions stipulated, and the Board's actions were to secure compliance with environmental standards.
Case: Andhra Pradesh Pollution Control Board vs. CCL Products (India) Limited
Date: 22nd July 2019

Q: What was the main issue in the case of Rojer Mathew vs. South Indian Bank Limited & Ors.?
A: The main issue was the restructuring of the Tribunal system in India to ensure independence, effectiveness, and accessibility, as per the constitutional scheme and judicial precedents.
Case: Rojer Mathew vs. South Indian Bank Limited & Ors.
Date: 7th May 2018

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court note about the functioning of Tribunals in India?
A: The Supreme Court noted that the functioning of Tribunals required a review to ensure they provided speedy and inexpensive quality justice, and that they must adhere to principles of independence and separation of powers.
Case: Rojer Mathew vs. South Indian Bank Limited & Ors.
Date: 7th May 2018

---

Q: What were the concerns raised in previous judgements like R.K. Jain vs. Union of India and L. Chandra Kumar vs. Union of India?
A: Concerns raised included the lack of competence, objectivity, and judicial approach of Tribunal personnel, the need for judicial members to man Tribunals, and the importance of judicial review by High Courts over Tribunal decisions.
Case: Rojer Mathew vs. South Indian Bank Limited & Ors.
Date: 7th May 2018

---

Q: What recommendations did the Law Commission and Parliamentary Standing Committee make regarding the Tribunal system?
A: The recommendations included the creation of a National Tribunal Commission to oversee all Tribunals, ensuring independence and fairness in appointments, and establishing uniform service conditions for Tribunal members.
Case: Rojer Mathew vs. South Indian Bank Limited & Ors.
Date: 7th May 2018

---

Q: What was the role of the amicus curiae, Shri Arvind P. Datar, in this case?
A: Shri Arvind P. Datar, as amicus curiae, assisted the court by providing a Concept Note suggesting the creation of a regular cadre for Tribunals, national competition for recruitment, and an independent oversight mechanism.
Case: Rojer Mathew vs. South Indian Bank Limited & Ors.
Date: 7th May 2018

---

Q: What were the Supreme Court's directives regarding the restructuring of Tribunals?
A: The Supreme Court directed the creation of a committee to oversee the restructuring of Tribunals, emphasizing the need for an autonomous body to handle appointments, performance review, and discipline of Tribunal members.
Case: Rojer Mathew vs. South Indian Bank Limited & Ors.
Date: 7th May 2018

---

Q: What were the key issues identified by the Supreme Court for consideration in restructuring the Tribunal system?
A: Key issues included creating a regular cadre for Tribunals, setting up an autonomous oversight body, amending the scheme of direct appeals to the Supreme Court, and making Tribunal Benches accessible at convenient locations.
Case: Rojer Mathew vs. South Indian Bank Limited & Ors.
Date: 7th May 2018

Q: What was the High Court's decision regarding the appellants' claim for absorption in the Minority Welfare Department?

Q: What was the High Court's ruling on the DNA test ordered by the Family Court?
A: The High Court upheld the Family Court's order for a DNA test, stating that the direction did not violate fundamental rights and that a DNA test was a legitimate means to establish the truth in the matter of paternity.
Case: Aparna Ajinkya Firodia vs. Ajinkya Arun Firodia
Date: 20th February 2023

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court view the interplay between Sections 112 and 114 of the Indian Evidence Act in this case?
A: The Supreme Court highlighted that Section 112 provides a presumption of legitimacy for children born during a valid marriage, which can only be rebutted by strong evidence of non-access. The Court also discussed that DNA tests should not be ordered routinely but only when absolutely necessary to resolve the controversy.
Case: Aparna Ajinkya Firodia vs. Ajinkya Arun Firodia
Date: 20th February 2023

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's final decision regarding the order for a DNA test?
A: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgement and the Family Court's order for a DNA test, stating that there was insufficient material to dislodge the presumption of legitimacy under Section 112 of the Indian Evidence Act, and that the DNA test was not justified in this case.
Case: Aparna Ajinkya Firodia vs. Ajinkya Arun Firodia
Date: 20th February 2023

Q: On what grounds did the Supreme Court of India overturn the High Court's decision in the case of Union of India & Ors. vs. Rajib Khan & Ors.?

---

Q: What were the key reasons provided by the Supreme Court for setting aside NLC's actions against S. Mahesh?
A: The Supreme Court reasoned that NLC had condoned the issue by allowing S. Mahesh to join and promoting him, making the caste certificate issue non-significant. It also highlighted that NLC's attempt to revoke the original punishment order after 13 years was legally unsustainable.
Case: S. Mahesh vs. The Chairman Cum Managing Director, Neyveli Lignite Corporation Ltd. Neyveli Tamil Nadu & Ors.
Date: 29th October 2018

---

Q: What was the High Court's decision regarding the status of the appellants as thika tenants in this case?
A: The High Court concluded that the appellants were not thika tenants of the property and that the Controller and the Tribunal were not justified in holding otherwise.
Case: Nemai Chandra Kumar (D) Thr. LRS. & Ors. vs. Mani Square Ltd. & Ors.
Date: 27th July 2022

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court interpret the term 'any structure' in the context of thika tenancy laws in this case?
A: The Supreme Court observed that the term 'any structure' in the context of thika tenancy laws should be interpreted to include only temporary or kutcha structures, and not permanent or pucca structures, which was crucial in determining the status of the appellants as thika tenants.
Case: Nemai Chandra Kumar (D) Thr. LRS. & Ors. vs. Mani Square Ltd. & Ors.
Date: 27th July 2022

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's final decision in the case of Nemai Chandra Kumar (D) Thr. LRS. & Ors. vs. Mani Square Ltd. & Ors.?
A: The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, concluding that the appellants were not thika tenants and that the landlord's interest in the property did not vest in the State under the thika tenancy laws.
Case: Nemai Chandra Kumar (D) Thr. LRS. & Ors. vs. Mani Square Ltd. & Ors.
Date: 27th July 2022

---

Q: What impact did the retrospective amendment of Section 5 of the Act of 2001 have on the case?
A: The retrospective amendment of Section 5 of the Act of 2001 aimed to include various types of land within the ambit of thika tenancy laws, but the Supreme Court found that this amendment did not alter the fundamental requirement that thika tenants must have temporary or kutcha structures on the land.
Case: Nemai Chandra Kumar (D) Thr. LRS. & Ors. vs. Mani Square Ltd. & Ors.
Date: 27th July 2022

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's decision regarding the payment of AGR dues by telecom service providers?
A: The Supreme Court mandated that telecom service providers must pay the AGR dues as calculated by the Department of Telecommunications without any reassessment or recalculation.
Case: Union of India vs. Association of Unified Telecom Service Providers of India
Date: 1st September 2020

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court view the applicability of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code to spectrum and AGR dues?
A: The Supreme Court held that the spectrum cannot be subjected to insolvency proceedings as it is not an operational asset but a state-owned asset under the Indian Telegraph Act. The dues towards the spectrum use are not operational dues under the IBC.
Case: Union of India vs. Association of Unified Telecom Service Providers of India
Date: 1st September 2020

---

Q: What guidelines did the Supreme Court provide for the payment of AGR dues?
A: The Supreme Court provided that telecom operators must pay 10% of their total dues by 31st March 2021 and the remaining amount in yearly installments over the next 20 years.
Case: Union of India vs. Association of Unified Telecom Service Providers of India
Date: 1st September 2020

---

Q: What was the impact of the Supreme Court's decision on non-telecom public sector undertakings (PSUs)?
A: The Supreme Court acknowledged that non-telecom PSUs, such as Powergrid, GAIL, and DMRC, are not involved in providing telecom services to the public and decided to withdraw the demands raised for license fees based on non-telecom revenue.
Case: Union of India vs. Association of Unified Telecom Service Providers of India
Date: 1st September 2020

---

Q: What was the High Court's decision regarding the impleadment of Jayeshkumar Chhakaddas Shah (JCS) in the suit?

Q: What was the Supreme Court's view on the effect of the legal heirs of MMT withdrawing the suit?
A: The Supreme Court held that JCS had a vital interest in the suit and was entitled to continue the suit despite the legal heirs of MMT compromising the matter and withdrawing from the suit.
Case: Pruthvirajsinh Nodhubha Jadeja vs. Jayeshkumar Chhakaddas Shah & Ors.
Date: 4th October 2019

Q: What was the Supreme Court's final decision in this case?

Q: What was the decision of the High Court of Karnataka regarding the rollback of the retirement age?
A: The High Court of Karnataka held that the rollback of the retirement age from 60 to 58 years was valid but stated that the rollback should not affect the existing rights recognized under clause 17(7)(iii) of the Certified Standing Orders.
Case: Chairman-cum-M.D. ITI Limited vs. K. Muniswamy & Ors.
Date: 2nd March 2023

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court decide regarding the interpretation of clause 17(7)(iii) of the Certified Standing Orders?
A: The Supreme Court held that clause 17(7)(iii) is an enabling provision that allows the appellant to continue an employee in service up to the age of 60 years, subject to medical fitness, but it does not confer any right on employees to seek continuation as a matter of right.
Case: Chairman-cum-M.D. ITI Limited vs. K. Muniswamy & Ors.
Date: 2nd March 2023

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court modify the High Court's judgment in this case?
A: The Supreme Court modified the High Court's judgment by clarifying that clause 17(7)(iii) of the Certified Standing Orders does not confer any right on employees to seek continuation in service till the age of 60 years, and the clause only provides discretionary power to the appellant.
Case: Chairman-cum-M.D. ITI Limited vs. K. Muniswamy & Ors.
Date: 2nd March 2023

---

Q: What was the final outcome of the Supreme Court's decision regarding the appeal?
A: The Supreme Court partly allowed the appeal, upholding the validity of the rollback of the retirement age and clarifying the interpretation of clause 17(7)(iii) while dismissing any claims for continuation of employment based on this clause.
Case: Chairman-cum-M.D. ITI Limited vs. K. Muniswamy & Ors.
Date: 2nd March 2023

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court decide regarding the High Court's dismissal of Khilendra Singh's writ petition?
A: The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court's conclusion ,that Khilendra Singh was not entitled to appointment in a post reserved for OBCs since the Jaat caste was not in the Central List of OBCs at the relevant time, though the Supreme Court provided different reasons for upholding the decision.

Date: 6th May 2024

Q: What was the Bihar Superior Judicial Service Rules, 1951 amended to include?

Date: 6th May 2024

Q: What was the decision of the court regarding the merit of the appeals filed by Shankar and others?

Q: On what basis were the appointments of the candidates corrected by the High Court?

Q: What was the primary issue in the appeal by The State of Bihar against Dr. Sachindra Narayan?
A: The primary issue was the direction by the High Court to provide financial assistance for payment of arrears and current pension to the employees of the Anugraha Narayan Sinha Institute of Social Studies, Patna.
Case: The State of Bihar & Anr. vs. Dr. Sachindra Narayan & Ors.
Date: 30th January 2019

---

Q: What did the Division Bench of the High Court of Patna order on 13th March 2018 regarding the Anugraha Narayan Sinha Institute?
A: The Division Bench ordered the appellant to provide financial assistance for payment of arrears and current pension to the employees of the Institute.
Case: The State of Bihar & Anr. vs. Dr. Sachindra Narayan & Ors.
Date: 30th January 2019

---

Q: What was the High Court's reasoning for allowing the writ petition and directing the State to pay pensions?
A: The High Court allowed the writ petition on the grounds that the State Government had earmarked grants under the pension head in previous years and had provided funds for the payment of pensions, thereby creating a legitimate expectation for the employees that they would receive pensions.
Case: The State of Bihar & Anr. vs. Dr. Sachindra Narayan & Ors.
Date: 30th January 2019

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's decision regarding the High Court's order on pension payments?
A: The Supreme Court found that the order of the Division Bench of the High Court was not legally sustainable and allowed the appeal, dismissing the writ petition and ruling that the State Government was not obligated to pay the pensions as the retirement benefit scheme was to be operated from the Institute's own resources.
Case: The State of Bihar & Anr. vs. Dr. Sachindra Narayan & Ors.
Date: 30th January 2019

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court say about the doctrine of legitimate expectation in this case?
A: The Supreme Court stated that legitimate expectation cannot be claimed as a right and must be founded on the sanction of law or custom or an established procedure. The past payment of pensions by the State did not create an enforceable right for the Institute or its employees.
Case: The State of Bihar & Anr. vs. Dr. Sachindra Narayan & Ors.
Date: 30th January 2019

---

Date: 5th December 2017

Case: Revanasiddayya vs. Gangamma @ Shashikala & Anr.
Date: 5th December 2017

Q: What was the primary legal challenge in the writ petition filed by Lok Prahari?
A: The primary legal challenge was the validity of Section 4(3) of the Uttar Pradesh Ministers (Salaries, Allowances and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1981, as amended in 2016, which allowed former Chief Ministers to retain government accommodation for their lifetime.
Case: Lok Prahari through its general secretary vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.
Date: 7th May 2018

---

Q: What did the 1997 Rules regarding accommodation for former Chief Ministers state?
A: The 1997 Rules provided for the allotment of government accommodation to former Chief Ministers for their lifetime. However, these rules were struck down by the High Court earlier as being in conflict with the provisions of Section 4 of the 1981 Act.
Case: Lok Prahari through its general secretary vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.
Date: 7th May 2018

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's ruling on the validity of Section 4(3) of the 1981 Act?
A: The Supreme Court ruled that Section 4(3) of the 1981 Act was unconstitutional as it violated the equality clause under Article 14 of the Constitution of India. The court held that the provision created an arbitrary classification by treating former Chief Ministers as a special category, which was not supported by any constitutional principle.
Case: Lok Prahari through its general secretary vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.
Date: 7th May 2018

---

Q: What broader principles did the Supreme Court refer to in its judgment?
A: The Supreme Court referred to principles of equality and fraternity embodied in the Constitution, stating that public servants must act in a manner reflecting that ultimate authority is vested in the citizens. The court emphasized that privileges, rights, and benefits conferred on holders of public office must be reasonable, rational, and proportionate.
Case: Lok Prahari through its general secretary vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.
Date: 7th May 2018

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court say about the classification of former Chief Ministers as a special category of citizens?
A: The Supreme Court stated that once individuals demit public office, they are at par with common citizens. The court held that the classification of former Chief Ministers as a special category for the purpose of allotting government accommodation was arbitrary and discriminatory, thus violating Article 14 of the Constitution.
Case: Lok Prahari through its general secretary vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.
Date: 7th May 2018

---

Q: What was the High Court of Delhi's decision regarding the eligibility of ICDs for tax deductions?
A: The High Court of Delhi held that the ICDs operated by Container Corporation of India Ltd. were eligible for deductions under Section 80-IA of the Income Tax Act, 1961.
Case: Commissioner of Income Tax, Delhi vs. M/s Container Corporation of India Ltd.
Date: 24th April 2018

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court rule on the issue of ICDs being classified as 'inland ports'?
A: The Supreme Court ruled that ICDs could be considered 'inland ports' for the purposes of Section 80-IA(4) of the Income Tax Act, based on their function and the notifications issued by the Central Board of Excise and Customs and the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.
Case: Commissioner of Income Tax, Delhi vs. M/s Container Corporation of India Ltd.
Date: 24th April 2018

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's decision regarding the appeal filed by the Commissioner of Income Tax?
A: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's decision that Container Corporation of India Ltd. was entitled to claim deductions under Section 80-IA for the income earned from the ICDs.
Case: Commissioner of Income Tax, Delhi vs. M/s Container Corporation of India Ltd.
Date: 24th April 2018

---

Q: What reasoning did the Supreme Court provide for allowing the tax deduction for ICDs?
A: The Supreme Court reasoned that the ICDs performed functions similar to those of ports, such as customs clearance, and were notified as 'infrastructure facilities' by the CBDT. Therefore, they qualified for tax deductions under Section 80-IA(4) of the Income Tax Act.
Case: Commissioner of Income Tax, Delhi vs. M/s Container Corporation of India Ltd.
Date: 24th April 2018

Q: What was the argument presented by Life Insurance Corporation of India regarding the legislative competence of the state?
A: Life Insurance Corporation of India argued that the state of Rajasthan lacked legislative competence to impose stamp duty on insurance policies, as this power lies exclusively with the Parliament under Entry 91 of List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India.
Case: Life Insurance Corporation of India vs. The State of Rajasthan & Ors.
Date: 30th April 2024

---

Q: What was the decision of the High Court of Rajasthan regarding the imposition of stamp duty on insurance policies?
A: The High Court of Rajasthan upheld the imposition of stamp duty by the state government, stating that the state had the legislative competence to levy and collect stamp duty on insurance policies under the Rajasthan Stamp Law (Adaptation) Act, 1952.
Case: Life Insurance Corporation of India vs. The State of Rajasthan & Ors.
Date: 30th April 2024

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court rule on the issue of legislative competence regarding stamp duty on insurance policies?
A: The Supreme Court ruled that the state of Rajasthan has the legislative competence to impose and collect stamp duty on insurance policies issued within the state, as per Entry 44 of List III, and the rate prescribed by the Parliament under Entry 91 of List I.
Case: Life Insurance Corporation of India vs. The State of Rajasthan & Ors.
Date: 30th April 2024

---

Q: What relief was granted to the appellant by the Supreme Court despite upholding the state's power to levy stamp duty?
A: The Supreme Court granted relief to the appellant by setting aside certain findings of the High Court and directing the state government not to demand and collect the specific amounts of stamp duty as per the orders dated 16.09.2004, 16.10.2004, 11.10.2004, 01.11.2004, and 28.10.2004.
Case: Life Insurance Corporation of India vs. The State of Rajasthan & Ors.
Date: 30th April 2024

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court say about the applicability of the 1952 Act in the present case?
A: The Supreme Court held that the Rajasthan Stamp Law (Adaptation) Act, 1952 applies to the present case, as the insurance policies were issued between 1993-94 and 2001-02, prior to the 1998 Act coming into force.
Case: Life Insurance Corporation of India vs. The State of Rajasthan & Ors.
Date: 30th April 2024

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's stance on recalculating AGR dues?
A: The Supreme Court made it clear that there was no scope for raising any further dispute with respect to AGR dues, and no recalculation or self-assessment could be undertaken. The amounts stated were to be treated as final.
Case: Union of India vs. Association of Unified Telecom Service Providers of India and Ors.

---

Q: What were the main directions given by the Supreme Court in the order dated 01.09.2020?
A: The directions included: Telecom Operators cannot raise disputes on AGR dues, must pay 10% of the total dues by 31.03.2021, make yearly payments from 01.04.2021 to 31.03.2031, furnish undertakings to pay arrears, keep existing bank guarantees alive until payment is complete, and report compliance annually by 7th April.
Case: Union of India vs. Association of Unified Telecom Service Providers of India and Ors.

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's view on the potential impact of correcting arithmetical errors in AGR dues?
A: The Supreme Court viewed that correcting arithmetical errors would lead to recalculation, effectively altering the AGR dues specified in the previous order, which was not permissible as per their judgment.
Case: Union of India vs. Association of Unified Telecom Service Providers of India and Ors.

A: The private medical colleges challenged Rule 12 (8) (a) as it prevented them from filling up seats that fell vacant due to candidates not taking admission or resigning after the mop-up round, which they argued was an unreasonable restriction on their right to occupation under Article 19 (1) (g) of the Constitution of India.

Q: What was the High Court's initial ruling regarding the exchange deed?

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's final decision in this case?
A: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment, ruling that the exchange deed was indeed in contravention of the U.P. ZA & LR Act and thus void. The Court emphasized that the statutory provisions under Sections 157-B and 161 must be followed to protect the interests of Scheduled Tribes.
Case: Additional Commissioner Revenue and Others vs Akhalaq Hussain and Another

Q: What was the High Court's decision regarding the writ petition filed by M/S Godrej Sara Lee Ltd.?
A: The High Court dismissed the writ petition and relegated M/S Godrej Sara Lee Ltd. to the remedy of an appeal under section 33 of the Haryana Value Added Tax Act, 2003, citing the availability of an alternative remedy.
Case: M/S Godrej Sara Lee Ltd. vs. The Excise and Taxation Officer-cum-Assessing Authority & Ors.

---

Q: What were the reasons given by the Supreme Court for setting aside the High Court's decision?
A: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's decision because the jurisdictional issue raised by the appellant was a pure question of law and deserved consideration on merits. The Supreme Court noted that the High Court had mistakenly relied on the Titagarh Paper Mills case and failed to examine the appellant's claim that the orders impugned were passed wholly without jurisdiction.
Case: M/S Godrej Sara Lee Ltd. vs. The Excise and Taxation Officer-cum-Assessing Authority & Ors.

---

Q: What legal principle did the Supreme Court highlight regarding the exercise of writ powers under Article 226 of the Constitution?
A: The Supreme Court highlighted that the power to issue prerogative writs under Article 226 is plenary and any limitation must be traceable in the Constitution itself. It emphasized that mere availability of an alternative remedy does not bar the maintainability of a writ petition and that high courts have discretion in deciding whether to entertain a writ petition.
Case: M/S Godrej Sara Lee Ltd. vs. The Excise and Taxation Officer-cum-Assessing Authority & Ors.

---

Q: What was the final decision of the Supreme Court regarding the impugned orders of the Revisional Authority?
A: The Supreme Court invalidated the impugned final revisional orders dated 2nd March, 2009 for the assessment years 2003-04 and 2004-05, holding that the Revisional Authority exceeded its jurisdiction. The Court restored the orders of the Assessing Authority and made the interim order dated 18th January, 2010 absolute.
Case: M/S Godrej Sara Lee Ltd. vs. The Excise and Taxation Officer-cum-Assessing Authority & Ors.

---

Q: Why did the High Court quash the circular dated 23.05.2009?
A: The High Court quashed the circular dated 23.05.2009 because it was issued without authority or competence and without the approval of the Finance Department, leading to financial implications for the State.
Case: M.P. Medical Officers Association vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.

---

Q: What was the Division Bench of the High Court's decision regarding the recovery of excess amounts paid to the Medical Officers?
A: The Division Bench of the High Court upheld the recovery of the excess amounts paid along with interest, stating that the benefits granted under the circular dated 23.05.2009 were without proper authorization.
Case: M.P. Medical Officers Association vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's decision regarding the recovery of excess amounts paid?
A: The Supreme Court quashed the recovery of the excess amounts paid between 2009 and 2012, noting that the recovery was unjustified as the benefits were granted without any misrepresentation or fault on the part of the employees.
Case: M.P. Medical Officers Association vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.

---

Q: What instructions did the Supreme Court give regarding the pay fixation and pension of the employees?
A: The Supreme Court instructed that the pay fixation and pension of the employees should be worked out as per the order dated 26.08.2008, as if the circular dated 23.05.2009 was never issued.
Case: M.P. Medical Officers Association vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh & Ors.

---

Q: What was the sole ground on which the High Court allowed the writ petition in the Mahesh Kumar Agarwal case?
A: The High Court allowed the writ petition on the ground that the appellant-landlord had not given a six-month notice prior to filing the eviction application, as required under Section 21(1)(a) of the Act.
Case: Mahesh Kumar Agarwal (Dead) By LRS v. Naresh Chandra & Ors.

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's decision regarding the period of limitation?
A: The Supreme Court decided that the period of limitation for filing appeals under section 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, should not exceed 120 days, including a grace period of 30 days under section 5 of the Limitation Act, aligning with the objective of speedy resolution of disputes in arbitration.
Case: Government of Maharashtra (Water Resources Department) vs M/S Borse Brothers Engineers & Contractors Pvt. Ltd.

---

Q: What was the outcome of the appeals filed by the Government of Maharashtra and Union of India?
A: The appeals filed by the Government of Maharashtra and Union of India were dismissed by the High Courts of Bombay and Delhi, respectively, for failing to condone the delay in filing the appeals beyond the 120-day period.
Case: Government of Maharashtra (Water Resources Department) vs M/S Borse Brothers Engineers & Contractors Pvt. Ltd.

---

Q: What is the primary issue challenged in the case Janhit Abhiyan vs. Union of India & Ors.?
A: The primary issue challenged is the constitutional validity of The Constitution (One Hundred and Third Amendment) Act, 2019, which introduced Articles 15(6) and 16(6) providing reservation for economically weaker sections.
Case: Janhit Abhiyan vs. Union of India & Ors.

---

Q: What amendments were made to the Constitution by The Constitution (One Hundred and Third Amendment) Act, 2019?
A: The amendments included the insertion of clause (6) in Article 15 and clause (6) in Article 16, allowing the state to make special provisions for the advancement of economically weaker sections, including reservations in educational institutions and public employment up to 10%.
Case: Janhit Abhiyan vs. Union of India & Ors.

---

Q: On what grounds do the petitioners argue that the amendments are unconstitutional?
A: The petitioners argue that the amendments alter the basic structure of the Constitution by allowing reservations based solely on economic criteria, which they claim runs contrary to the principles established in the Indra Sawhney case and violates the 50% cap on reservations.
Case: Janhit Abhiyan vs. Union of India & Ors.

---

Q: What justification did the Union of India provide for the amendments?
A: The Union of India justified the amendments by stating that they aim to benefit economically weaker sections of society not covered by existing reservation schemes, arguing that this promotes social equality and aligns with the directive principles of the Constitution.
Case: Janhit Abhiyan vs. Union of India & Ors.

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's decision regarding the necessity of referring the case to a larger bench?
A: The Supreme Court decided to refer the case to a Constitution Bench of five Judges, acknowledging that it involves substantial questions of law regarding the interpretation of the Constitution and the basic structure doctrine.
Case: Janhit Abhiyan vs. Union of India & Ors.

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's decision regarding the application of the amended rules?
A: The Supreme Court set aside the Division Bench's order, stating that the appellant could not be penalized for his conduct in 2007 under the amended rules of 2010.
Case: Arun Kumar Niranjan vs. District Basic Education Officer & Ors.

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court decide regarding the costs of the case?
A: The Supreme Court vacated the order on costs passed by the learned Single Judge.
Case: Arun Kumar Niranjan vs. District Basic Education Officer & Ors.

---

Q: What was the primary issue raised by Common Cause in the writ petition?
A: The primary issue raised by Common Cause in the writ petition was seeking a writ of mandamus to direct the Union of India to appoint a regular Director of CBI by following the procedure laid down in section 4A of the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946, and to quash the order dated 10th January 2019 appointing Mr. Nageshwar Rao as the interim Director of CBI.
Case: Common Cause & Anr. vs Union of India & Anr.

---

Q: What did the petitioners allege about the appointment of Mr. Nageshwar Rao as interim Director of CBI?
A: The petitioners alleged that the appointment of Mr. Nageshwar Rao as interim Director of CBI was made in an arbitrary and illegal manner, bypassing the High Powered Selection Committee and not following the procedure established by the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946.
Case: Common Cause & Anr. vs Union of India & Anr.

---

Q: How did the court respond to the petitioners' claims about the lack of transparency in the CBI Director's appointment process?
A: The court found that the appointment of the interim Director had been authorised by the Committee under section 4A of the DSPE Act, and therefore, the claims about the lack of transparency and unauthorised appointment were fallacious. The court dismissed the writ petition, stating that there was no ground to interfere.
Case: Common Cause & Anr. vs Union of India & Anr.

---

Q: What did the petitioners request regarding the records of the CBI Director's appointment process?
A: The petitioners requested that all records of deliberations and rational criteria for shortlisting and selecting the Director of CBI be properly recorded and made available to citizens in accordance with the RTI Act, to ensure transparency in the shortlisting, selection, and appointment process.
Case: Common Cause & Anr. vs Union of India & Anr.

---

Q: What was the outcome of the writ petition filed by Common Cause?
A: The writ petition filed by Common Cause was dismissed by the court. The court found no grounds to interfere with the appointment of the interim Director of CBI, stating that the main prayer of the petitioners had been satisfied with the appointment of a regular Director, and the petitioners' claims were found to be without merit.
Case: Common Cause & Anr. vs Union of India & Anr.

---

Q: What condition did the High Court impose while setting aside the ex-parte decree?
A: The High Court imposed the condition that the petitioners/defendants pay a sum of Rs. 2,50,000/- to the decree holders, representing the amount spent on purchasing stamp papers and other expenses.
Case: K.P. Natarajan & Anr. vs. Muthalammal & Ors.

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's stance on the High Court's use of Article 227 in this case?
A: The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's use of Article 227, stating that the High Court's powers under Article 227 are broader and can include setting aside an ex-parte decree, especially when the interests of a minor are involved.
Case: K.P. Natarajan & Anr. vs. Muthalammal & Ors.

---

Q: What were the key grounds of the petitioners' challenge against the High Court's decision?
A: The petitioners challenged the High Court's decision on grounds that it should not have set aside the ex-parte decree in a revision petition related to condonation of delay, that the High Court should not have invoked equity in favor of the negligent respondents, and that the issue of appointment of a guardian was not raised by the respondents in their revision petition.
Case: K.P. Natarajan & Anr. vs. Muthalammal & Ors.

---

Q: What did the court decide regarding the inclusion of various charges in the value for the purpose of levy of duty?
A: The court held that the price charged for a manufactured article at the stage when the article enters into the stream of trade in order to determine the value/transaction value for the computation of the quantum of excise duty payable can include certain value additions and inclusions which enrich the value of the product to make it suitable for sale or to facilitate such sale. Doing so does not introduce any inconsistency between the nature and character of the levy and the measure adopted.
Case: Commissioner of Central Excise, Indore vs M/S Grasim Industries Ltd.

---

Q: What relief was sought by Prem Singh in his writ petition filed in the High Court?
A: Prem Singh sought to count the period spent in the work-charged establishment as qualifying service under the Rules of 1965 for the purpose of pension. His initial representation and subsequent representations were rejected, leading to the filing of the writ petition.
Case: Prem Singh vs. State of Uttar Pradesh

---

Q: What precedent cases did Prem Singh rely on in his appeal?
A: Prem Singh relied on the decision of the Supreme Court in Habib Khan vs. State of Uttarakhand and other cases where the period of work-charged service was counted as qualifying service for pension.
Case: Prem Singh vs. State of Uttar Pradesh

---

Q: What was the primary question considered by the Supreme Court in this case?

Q: Why did the Supreme Court allow the appeals filed by the College?
A: The Supreme Court allowed the appeals because the High Court erred in its judgment by not recognizing that the respondents were appointed on a part-time basis and did not work beyond April 1990, thus having no right to be regularized as Lecturers.

Q: What was the result of the compliance with the High Court's order by the Directorate of Higher Education?
A: The Directorate of Higher Education passed an order on 6th August 1996, holding that the respondents had not applied in terms of the advertisement and were appointed as part-time Lecturers, thus had no provision in the Act for regularizing their services.
Case: Committee of Management vs. The Director of Higher Education & Ors.

Q: What was the main issue in the case of St. Mary's Education Society & Anr. vs. Rajendra Prasad Bhargava & Ors.?

Q: What was the High Court of Karnataka's decision regarding the betterment fee levied by the Bangalore International Airport Area Planning Authority?
A: The High Court of Karnataka set aside the order passed by the Single Judge and held that the betterment fee levied by the Bangalore International Airport Area Planning Authority was not sustainable as the industrial area and its development were governed by the KIAD Act, not the KTCP Act.
Case: Bangalore International Airport Area Planning Authority vs Birla Super Bulk Terminal (Now a unit of Ultra Tech Cement Ltd.) and Ors.

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's decision in this case?
A: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment and held that the Bangalore International Airport Area Planning Authority had the authority to levy betterment charges. The respondent was directed to pay the levied amount of Rs. 1,48,29,173/- with interest.
Case: Bangalore International Airport Area Planning Authority vs Birla Super Bulk Terminal (Now a unit of Ultra Tech Cement Ltd.) and Ors.

---

Q: Why did the Supreme Court find the High Court's reasoning contradictory?
A: The Supreme Court found the High Court's reasoning contradictory because, on one hand, the High Court held that the KTCP Act did not apply to industrial areas governed by the KIAD Act, while on the other hand, it required the respondent to obtain approval from the Planning Authority under the KTCP Act. This contradiction implied that the planning authority had jurisdiction but was simultaneously denied the authority to levy fees.
Case: Bangalore International Airport Area Planning Authority vs Birla Super Bulk Terminal (Now a unit of Ultra Tech Cement Ltd.) and Ors.

---

Q: What was the decision of the High Court that the Supreme Court reviewed?
A: The High Court had dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant under Article 227 of the Constitution against the order dated 09.01.1997 of the Maharashtra Revenue Tribunal, and also rejected the review petition filed against the same.
Case: Bayaji Sambhu Mali @ Borate(D) Through LRS. vs. Nazir Mohammed Balal Zari Through GPA Holder & Ors.

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court conclude regarding the appellant's status as a deemed purchaser?
A: The Supreme Court concluded that the appellant was indeed a deemed purchaser due to the rejection of the landlord's application for possession filed within the statutory period after attaining majority, thus negating the need for the appellant to issue a notice under Section 32F(1A).
Case: Bayaji Sambhu Mali @ Borate(D) Through LRS. vs. Nazir Mohammed Balal Zari Through GPA Holder & Ors.

---

Q: What were the Supreme Court's findings regarding the transactions executed by the respondents?
A: The Supreme Court found that the transactions executed by the respondents were illegal due to the doctrine of lis pendens, and rejected the defence of the respondents 1-2 as bonafide purchasers for valuable consideration.
Case: Chander Bhan (D) through LR Sher Singh vs Mukhtiar Singh & Ors.

---

Q: What was the final decision of the Supreme Court in this case?
A: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the judgment of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, upheld the decree in favour of the appellant, and directed respondent no. 3 to accept the balance sale consideration and execute the agreement to sell within three months.
Case: Chander Bhan (D) through LR Sher Singh vs Mukhtiar Singh & Ors.

Q: What is the significance of the impugned judgment dated 22nd October 2013 in this case?
A: The impugned judgment dated 22nd October 2013 of the Patna High Court agreed with the Advance Rulings Authority and rejected the case of the Appellant under Section 3(2) second proviso of the Entry Tax Act, stating that the set-off would not be allowable under the aforesaid proviso.
Case: Indian Oil Corporation Limited vs State of Bihar & Anr.

---

Q: What were the five questions framed by the Patna High Court in the judgment dated 19th April 2017?
A: The five questions were: (i) Whether the second proviso to Section 3(2) of the Entry Tax Act is ultra vires to the Constitution? (ii) Whether interest can be levied in the matter of late payment of entry tax under the Entry Tax Act, by virtue of the provisions of the Bihar Finance Act, and, with the aid of Section 8 of the Entry Tax Act? (iii) Whether entry tax is liable to be paid when the goods only enter the local area and after such entry is subjected to sell only without there being any use or consumption of the goods in the local area? (iv) Whether based on audit objection as contemplated under the provisions of Section 33 of the VAT Act, assessment can be re-opened with the aid of Section 8 of the Entry Tax Act? (v) Whether the assessment undertaken under Section 33 of the VAT Act is permissible after a period of four years in view of the provision of Section 31 of the VAT Act?
Case: Indian Oil Corporation Limited vs State of Bihar & Anr.

---

Q: What was the outcome of the five questions framed by the Patna High Court?
A: Questions 1, 3, 4, and 5 were answered against the assessee (Indian Oil Corporation Limited), while question 2 was answered in its favour, stating that since there was no substantive provision by which interest could be levied, the interest charged to the Appellant by the assessment orders in question would have to be set aside.
Case: Indian Oil Corporation Limited vs State of Bihar & Anr.

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's decision regarding the levy of interest on the Entry Tax demand?
A: The Supreme Court decided that interest could not be levied as there was no substantive statutory provision for the same. This finding, having become final, could not be interfered with. The Court also declined to grant restitutional interest to the Revenue, citing the inequity of allowing the State to charge interest under the circumstances.
Case: Indian Oil Corporation Limited vs State of Bihar & Anr.

Q: What was the primary issue in the case of Dr. NTR University of Health Sciences vs. Dr. Yerra Trinadh & Others?

Q: What was the decision of the High Court of Andhra Pradesh that led to the appeal?

Q: What was the Supreme Court's stance on the High Court's order for re-evaluation?

Q: What was the main issue in the revision petition filed in the High Court of Madras?
A: The main issue in the revision petition was the order passed by the Executing Court on 19th September 2005, which directed the possession of the suit property to be given to Varadarajan as the legal representative of Umadevi, based on a decree in favor of Umadevi.
Case: Varadarajan vs. Kanakavalli & Ors.

---

Q: What was the decision of the High Court regarding the Will executed by Umadevi?
A: The High Court found that the execution of the Will was surrounded by suspicious circumstances and concluded that the Will had not been proved genuine. Consequently, the legatee under the said Will could not be considered a legal representative to maintain the execution petition.
Case: Varadarajan vs. Kanakavalli & Ors.

---

Q: What was the final decision of the Supreme Court regarding the order passed by the High Court?
A: The Supreme Court found that the High Court's order was not sustainable in law, set it aside, and restored the order of the Executing Court. The Supreme Court concluded that Varadarajan, as the legal representative of Umadevi, was entitled to execute the decree.
Case: Varadarajan vs. Kanakavalli & Ors.

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's decision regarding the Commission's order to charge interest on the balance amount?
A: The Supreme Court quashed and set aside the part of the Commission's order that allowed the respondent-developer to charge interest @9% per annum on the balance amount from the appellants. The Court directed the respondents to convey the outstanding amount to the appellants within two months, and the possession of the flat should be handed over within 30 days of the final payment.
Case: Sanjay Chaudhary and Anr. vs. Pioneer Urban Land & Infrastructure Ltd. and Anr.

---

Q: What was the decision of the High Court of Delhi that was challenged in the Supreme Court in the case of Raj Kumar Bhatia vs Subhash Chander Bhatia?
A: The High Court of Delhi had set aside the Trial Court's order allowing the amendment of the appellant's written statement, which the appellant challenged in the Supreme Court.
Case: Raj Kumar Bhatia vs Subhash Chander Bhatia

---

Q: What were the grounds for the Supreme Court's decision in favor of Raj Kumar Bhatia regarding the amendment of the written statement?
A: The Supreme Court held that the proposed amendment was an elaboration of what was stated in the original written statement and that the High Court had overstepped its jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution by evaluating the merits of the case while considering the amendment application.
Case: Raj Kumar Bhatia vs Subhash Chander Bhatia

---

Q: What was the main issue in the appeal filed by Sau. Sangeeta W/O Sunil Shinde?
A: The main issue in the appeal was the challenge to the order passed by the District Collector, Ahmednagar, approving the selection of Dr. Vandana Dnyaneshwar Murkute as Gatneta (Group Leader) of the Indian National Congress, Shrirampur Panchayat Samiti Party (INCPS Party), which was upheld by the High Court of Judicature at Bombay, bench at Aurangabad.
Case: SAU. SANGEETA W/O SUNIL SHINDE vs THE STATE OF MAHARASHTRA AND ORS.

---

Q: What was the High Court's decision on the writ petition filed by the appellant?
A: The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant, holding that the decision to remove the appellant and appoint respondent 3 as Gatneta was in accordance with the rules and procedures of the INCPS Party.
Case: SAU. SANGEETA W/O SUNIL SHINDE vs THE STATE OF MAHARASHTRA AND ORS.

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court conclude regarding the appeal?
A: The Supreme Court concluded that the appellant had lost the support of the majority of the INCPS Party and thus could not continue as Gatneta. The Court upheld the High Court's decision and dismissed the appeal, emphasizing that in a democratic setup, the will of the majority must prevail.
Case: SAU. SANGEETA W/O SUNIL SHINDE vs THE STATE OF MAHARASHTRA AND ORS.

---

Q: What was the appellant challenging in the Supreme Court?
A: The appellant was challenging the award passed by the Lok Adalat before the High Court, where Original Suit No. 68 of 2010 had been compromised between the parties.
Case: Sudhir Kumar Jain vs. Neeraj Kumar Jain & Ors.

---

Q: What was the High Court's initial stance on the appellant's challenge?
A: The High Court was not inclined to interfere with the award on the ground that the appellant was not an aggrieved party.
Case: Sudhir Kumar Jain vs. Neeraj Kumar Jain & Ors.

---

Q: What issue is pending before the High Court related to this case?
A: The core issue regarding the settlement as per the Lok Adalat dated 2nd September 2013 is now pending before the High Court in Misc. Petition (C) No. 497 of 2018, in which both sides are parties.
Case: Sudhir Kumar Jain vs. Neeraj Kumar Jain & Ors.

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court decide regarding the impugned judgment dated 11th March 2015?
A: The Supreme Court set aside the impugned judgment dated 11th March 2015 and remitted the matter to the High Court to be taken along with Misc. Petition (C) No. 497 of 2018.
Case: Sudhir Kumar Jain vs. Neeraj Kumar Jain & Ors.

---

Q: What was the High Court's initial ruling on the matter?
A: The High Court initially ruled that the levy of user charges by the Municipal Corporation was not sustainable as it fell within the ambit of Section 88 of the Haryana Municipal Corporation Act, which required prior approval from the State Government.
Case: The Municipal Corporation, Faridabad vs. Modern School, Faridabad & Ors.

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court of India rule on the appeal by the Municipal Corporation, Faridabad?
A: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's order, and ruled that the Municipal Corporation was justified in levying user charges for the discharge of waste water from the schools' tubewells into the municipal sewer system.
Case: The Municipal Corporation, Faridabad vs. Modern School, Faridabad & Ors.

---

Q: What legal provisions did the Supreme Court consider in making its decision?
A: The Supreme Court considered various sections of the Haryana Municipal Corporation Act, including Section 43, which mandates the corporation's responsibilities for drainage and sewage disposal, and Section 205, which requires permission for any connection to municipal drains.
Case: The Municipal Corporation, Faridabad vs. Modern School, Faridabad & Ors.

---

Q: What was the decision of the High Court in this case?
A: The High Court dismissed the second appeal filed by the State of Orissa, ruling in favor of the plaintiffs. The Court found that there was no material to support the Collector's conclusion that the terms of the lease had been violated and that the State had not demonstrated that the lease was determined in accordance with the lease agreement.
Case: State of Orissa vs. Santi Kumar Mitra & Another

---

Q: What was the decision of the High Court regarding the counting of work charged service for pension purposes?
A: The High Court held that for pension purposes, only the period of work charged service that makes up the shortfall in qualifying service should be counted, using the rule of one year for every five years of work charged service, rather than counting the entire work charged service period.
Case: Uday Pratap Thakur and Anr. vs. The State of Bihar and Ors.

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's stance on the entire service period being considered for pension calculation?
A: The Supreme Court held that the entire period of work charged service cannot be counted for pension calculation, as it would equate work charged employees with regular employees, which is not permissible.
Case: Uday Pratap Thakur and Anr. vs. The State of Bihar and Ors.

---

Q: What was the decision of the Kerala High Court regarding the tax exemption for residential accommodations for nuns?
A: The Kerala High Court decided that buildings used for the residence of nuns in a convent are principally used for religious purposes and therefore should qualify for exemption from building tax.
Case: Government of Kerala & Anr. vs. Mother Superior Adoration Convent

---

Q: How did the Supreme Court interpret the term 'principally used for' in relation to the Kerala Building Tax Act, 1975?
A: The Supreme Court interpreted 'principally used for' to mean that buildings used mainly for religious, charitable, or educational purposes should be exempt from building tax, even if they are not exclusively used for such purposes.
Case: Government of Kerala & Anr. vs. Mother Superior Adoration Convent

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's stance on the argument that exemption provisions in tax statutes should be construed strictly?
A: The Supreme Court acknowledged the general rule of strict interpretation for exemption provisions in tax statutes but emphasized that beneficial exemptions aimed at promoting certain activities should be construed liberally to fulfill their purpose.
Case: Government of Kerala & Anr. vs. Mother Superior Adoration Convent

---

Q: What was the final outcome of the appeals filed by the State of Kerala?
A: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals filed by the State of Kerala, upholding the decisions of the Division Bench and the Full Bench of the Kerala High Court that granted building tax exemptions to the buildings in question.
Case: Government of Kerala & Anr. vs. Mother Superior Adoration Convent

Q: What was the outcome of the High Court of Karnataka's decision on 26th May 2021?

Q: What was the outcome of the appeal to the Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT) regarding the SEBI order?

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court decide regarding the obligation to pay future interest in the case of Dushyant N. Dalal and Another?
A: The Supreme Court decided that since the SEBI order dated 21st July 2009 did not expressly award future interest and instead imposed a severe penalty of a seven-year market ban for non-payment within the stipulated time, no future interest was payable. The SAT's judgment that the appellants were obligated to pay interest until payment was set aside.
Case: Dushyant N. Dalal and Another vs. Securities and Exchange Board of India

Q: What was the decision of the Trial Court regarding the appellant's request for an extension of time to pay the balance of the sale consideration?

Q: What was the High Court's decision regarding Dr. Prabhugouda's CAS promotion date?
A: The High Court decided that Dr. Prabhugouda's CAS promotion should be effective from 01.01.2009, considering his previous service in an affiliated college.
Case: Registrar Karnataka University & Anr. vs Dr. Prabhugouda & Anr.

---

Q: Why did the Karnataka University challenge the High Court's decision?
A: Karnataka University challenged the decision because they believed the CAS promotion should only apply from the date Dr. Prabhugouda joined the University on 28.10.2013, not from when he worked in an affiliated college.
Case: Registrar Karnataka University & Anr. vs Dr. Prabhugouda & Anr.

---

Q: What was the Supreme Court's final ruling on the effective date of Dr. Prabhugouda's promotion?
A: The Supreme Court ruled that the effective date of Dr. Prabhugouda's promotion should be 28.10.2013, not 01.01.2009, as he was not in the service of the University during the earlier period.
Case: Registrar Karnataka University & Anr. vs Dr. Prabhugouda & Anr.

---

Q: What rationale did the Supreme Court provide for its decision?
A: The Supreme Court reasoned that promotions under CAS should only be effective from the date of entry into the University service, and Dr. Prabhugouda was not in the service of the University before 28.10.2013.
Case: Registrar Karnataka University & Anr. vs Dr. Prabhugouda & Anr.

---

Q: What did the Supreme Court say about the interpretation of the term 'colleges' in the statute?
A: The Supreme Court stated that the term 'colleges' in the statute refers only to 'constituent colleges' and not 'affiliated colleges', which influenced their decision regarding the promotion date.
Case: Registrar Karnataka University & Anr. vs Dr. Prabhugouda & Anr.

---

Q: What was the main issue addressed in the appeal by The Principal Commissioner of Income Tax?

Q: What was the High Court of Gujarat's decision regarding the revenue's appeal?
A: The High Court of Gujarat dismissed the revenue's appeal, stating that the proposed questions were not substantial questions of law and were based on factual aspects.

Q: Why did the Supreme Court find the High Court's order unsustainable?

---

Q: What action did the Supreme Court take regarding the High Court's decision?

---

Q: What directions did the Supreme Court give to the High Court for reconsidering the appeal?
A: The Supreme Court directed the High Court to pass a speaking and reasoned order after recording the submissions made on behalf of the respective parties and to consider whether the proposed questions of law were substantial or on factual aspects in accordance with the law.

Q: What was the Supreme Court's view on the admissibility of the statements made under Section 108 of the Customs Act?
A: The Supreme Court held that statements made under Section 108 of the Customs Act are admissible in evidence but must be recorded in a fair and judicious manner. The Court agreed with the CESTAT that the statements in this case were retracted at the earliest opportunity and could not be relied upon without corroborative evidence.
Case: Commissioner of Customs (Imports), Mumbai vs. M/S Ganpati Overseas through its proprietor Shri Yashpal Sharma & Anr.

---

Q: What was the final decision of the Supreme Court in this case?
A: The Supreme Court concurred with the CESTAT's decision, stating that the unattested photocopies of the initial export declarations could not form a reliable basis for enhancing the value of the goods. The Court upheld the CESTAT's judgment that the enhancement of the value of the imported goods and the penalties imposed could not be sustained.
Case: Commissioner of Customs (Imports), Mumbai vs. M/S Ganpati Overseas through its proprietor Shri Yashpal Sharma & Anr.
